title: Testing materials: how to run a fair test
playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat today. The rain bottle needs an air hole near its base, or it stops after a few drops, so the flow names that hole and practises over the medicine cup. 20 ml is used because a 1 cm dip in a patch over a tumbler holds only about 20 ml. The four tumblers are rained on one minute apart and each is lifted 4 minutes after its own rain, so every cloth waits the same time. One round takes about 9 minutes, so three rounds and the planning take about 55 minutes. The tiny cut test uses one layer of a paper napkin, because toilet paper has perforations, which are weak lines. Napkin strips 2 cm wide usually hold 10 to 40 coins, so 40 coins are enough. Hairs are wound round a pencil at the top and round the hook at the bottom before any knot, because a knot at the hook is a weak spot and the hair would break there. In the climbing water test the stick rests on two piles of books, because a stick lying on the tray's rim is too low for 15 cm strips. Haldi is not used to colour that water, because its tiny grains stay near the bottom of the strip while the water climbs on. Families short of coins can use level spoonfuls of dry rice instead. The spine is the umbrella patch test (one session of about 55 minutes), then the tiny cut test with the explanations, Roots and quiz (a second session of about 50 minutes). Cloth and paper results vary from home to home, and that is fine. The point is that the child plans the test, guesses with a reason first, and explains the result from what they saw.

summary.text: A shopkeeper says his umbrella cloth keeps out the most rain. How can you check? Pour the same amount of water on each cloth, from the same height, and wait the same time. Only the cloth is different, so any difference must come from the cloth. This is called a fair test. You also hang coins from strips of paper to test how strong they are. A strip with one small cut tears at the cut, because a material is only as strong as its weakest spot.
summary.art: A kitchen table laid out like a laboratory: four steel tumblers each covered with a different square of old cloth, a small plastic bottle dripping rain onto one of them, a medicine cup and a hand-drawn results table.

intro.hook: Your family must buy one umbrella for the monsoon. The shopkeeper says, 'This one is the most waterproof in all of India!' How could you find out if that is true, without just believing him?
intro.text: You cannot tell how waterproof a cloth is just by looking at it. You have to test it. A test means doing something to a material on purpose, and measuring what happens. A good test is fair. It gives every cloth the same chance, so only the cloth decides the result. Before you read on, think. How would you test four cloths so that nobody could call your test unfair? Keep your answer in mind. You are going to design that test yourself.
intro.art: A child in a shop doorway in the monsoon, looking doubtfully at a shopkeeper who holds up an open umbrella, with rain pouring down outside.

outcomes: I can plan a fair test myself: I decide what to change, what to keep the same and what to measure, before I start.
I can make a guess with a reason before a test, and check it against what happened.
I can test materials for how waterproof, strong, absorbent and springy they are, using exact amounts, a ruler, a medicine cup or a count.
I can record results in a table with clear headings and units, and show them in a bar chart.
I can repeat a test three times, find the middle value, and spot a result that does not fit.
I can explain why rain gets through a cloth at its biggest gaps, and why a strip tears first at a cut or a thin spot.
I can say what my test did not tell me, and why people test things before trusting them with their lives.

terms.meaning: What a thing is made of. Wood, steel, cotton, paper, plastic, rubber and glass are all materials.
terms.example: A steel tumbler is made of the material steel. A kurta is made of cotton. The unit 'What is it made of?' looks at where materials come from.
terms.art: A steel tumbler, a cotton kurta and a wooden spoon, each with a label pointing to its material.

terms.meaning: A word that says what a material is like, or what it can do. Waterproof, strong, stretchy and absorbent are properties. The unit on properties of materials compares many more of them.
terms.example: Rubber is stretchy. Plastic is waterproof. A paper towel is absorbent.
terms.art: A rubber band being stretched, a plastic sheet with water beading on it, and a paper towel soaking up a spill.

terms.meaning: Doing something to a material, on purpose, to find out what it can do. In a good test you measure the result.
terms.example: Pouring two spoons of water on a cloth and measuring how much comes through is a test.
terms.art: A child pouring a spoon of water onto a cloth stretched over a cup.

terms.meaning: A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same. Then you know what caused the difference.
terms.example: In the umbrella patch test, every cloth gets the same 20 ml of rain, from the same height. Every cloth waits the same time. Only the cloth changes.
terms.art: Three identical cups with three different cloths on top, the same spoon of water above each one.

terms.meaning: In a fair test, the one thing you change on purpose. In a materials test, it is usually the material. Scientists call it the independent variable.
terms.example: In the umbrella test, the thing we change is the cloth: cotton, plastic, newspaper or wool.
terms.art: Four squares of different cloth in a row, with a big arrow saying 'only this changes' drawn as a picture of a hand swapping them.

terms.term: The things we keep the same
terms.meaning: Everything else in the test. If one of these changes too, the test is not fair. Scientists call them control variables.
terms.example: The same cup, the same amount of water, the same time and the same size of cloth.
terms.art: A cup, a spoon, a timer and a ruler, each with a padlock drawn beside it.

terms.meaning: The result you look at and write down as a number. Scientists call it the dependent variable.
terms.example: How many millilitres of water came through the cloth. How many coins a paper strip held.
terms.art: A measuring cup with water in it, a pointing finger at the number on its side.

terms.meaning: A careful guess about what will happen, made before you test. You say why you think so.
terms.example: I predict the old jeans will let the least water through, because they are thick and I can't see light through them.
terms.art: A child with a thought bubble showing a plastic sheet with a tick, before a test starts.

terms.meaning: A grid for writing down what you found. Each column has a heading and a unit. Each row is one thing you tested.
terms.example: Columns: Material, Try 1 (ml), Try 2 (ml), Try 3 (ml), Middle value (ml).
terms.art: A neatly drawn table on paper with headings at the top and materials down the side.

terms.meaning: The size we count in when we measure. Centimetres (cm) for length, millilitres (ml) for water, grams (g) for weight.
terms.example: The paper strip was 2 cm wide. 12 ml of water came through the cotton hanky.
terms.art: A ruler showing cm, a measuring cup showing ml, and a kitchen scale showing g.

terms.meaning: A tiny amount of liquid. A teaspoon holds about 5 millilitres. A big glass of water holds about 250 millilitres.
terms.example: A medicine cup has lines for 5, 10, 15 and 20 millilitres.
terms.art: A teaspoon of water next to a small plastic medicine cup with lines marked on it.

terms.meaning: Doing the same test again, in exactly the same way. We usually do each test three times.
terms.example: We tested each paper strip three times, with a fresh strip each time.
terms.art: Three identical paper strips in a row, each holding a little bag of coins.

terms.meaning: Put your three results in order, smallest to biggest. The one in the middle is the middle value. Scientists call it the median.
terms.example: A strip held 9, 15 and 14 coins. In order: 9, 14, 15. The middle value is 14.
terms.art: Three number cards, 9, 14 and 15, in a row with the 14 in the middle glowing.

terms.meaning: A tiny weak spot in a material, such as a thin patch, a nick, a gap or a crack. Most flaws are too small to see.
terms.example: A pinhole in an umbrella is a flaw. Rain comes through there, even if the rest of the cloth is perfect.
terms.art: An umbrella held up against the sky, with one tiny bright pinhole of light shining through its dark cloth.

terms.meaning: Three sentences a scientist writes after a test. The claim is what I think. The evidence is what I saw. The reasoning is why I think it happened.
terms.example: Claim: old jeans make the best patch. Evidence: only 3 ml came through them. Reasoning: their threads are thick and packed tight, so the gaps are tiny.
terms.art: A notebook page with three lines, each beginning with a small picture: a speech bubble, an eye and a lightbulb.

terms.meaning: A result that is very different from the others, often because something went wrong. Scientists call it an anomaly. We check it, and test again.
terms.example: A strip held 14, 15 and 3 coins. The 3 is odd. Maybe that strip had a tiny tear.
terms.art: Three bars, two tall and one very short, with a magnifying glass over the short one.

terms.meaning: When you repeat a test and get nearly the same result each time, the results are reliable. You can trust them more.
terms.example: The cotton hanky let through 12, 13 and 12 ml. Those are close, so they are reliable.
terms.art: Three measuring cups with almost the same amount of water in each.

terms.meaning: Does not let water through.
terms.example: A plastic raincoat and an umbrella are waterproof.
terms.art: Raindrops bouncing off an umbrella, a child dry underneath.

terms.meaning: Soaks up water and holds it.
terms.example: A cotton towel, a sponge and a kitchen towel are absorbent.
terms.art: A kitchen towel soaking up a spilt glass of water on a table.

terms.meaning: How much pulling or weight a material can take before it breaks or tears.
terms.example: Brown paper bags hold more than tissue paper before they tear.
terms.art: A brown paper bag full of fruit beside a torn tissue.

terms.meaning: A stretchy material gets longer when you pull it, and goes back to its old length when you let go. Scientists call this elastic.
terms.example: A rubber band and the waistband of your pyjamas are elastic.
terms.art: A rubber band stretched long between two fingers, then short again.

terms.meaning: The load at which a material snaps or tears. Every material has one.
terms.example: One hair snapped when the bag hanging from it held 18 one-rupee coins.
terms.art: A thread snapping above a small bag of coins, with a little 'snap' star.

terms.meaning: How well a material stops itself being scratched. A harder material scratches a softer one.
terms.example: A metal key scratches chalk. Chalk cannot scratch the key.
terms.art: A steel key making a white scratch line on a stick of chalk.

terms.meaning: A very thin thread. Paper, cotton and wool are made of millions of fibres tangled or woven together.
terms.example: Tear a piece of paper and look at the edge with a magnifying glass. You can see tiny fibres sticking out.
terms.art: A magnified torn paper edge showing fluffy fibres like a tiny forest.

terms.meaning: A material made of very long chain-like molecules, like strings of beads. Rubber, plastic, cotton and silk are polymers.
terms.example: A rubber band is made of long, tangled chains that straighten out when you pull it.
terms.art: A zoom from a rubber band into a tangle of long bead chains, like cooked noodles.

terms.meaning: A tiny break in a material. A crack makes the material much weaker, because the force of a pull crowds at the crack's sharp tip.
terms.example: A milk packet has a small notch that says 'tear here'. The notch is a tiny crack, made on purpose.
terms.art: A milk packet with a small notch at the top and a tear running across from it.

terms.meaning: An agreed way of testing, or an agreed size, that everyone uses. Then tests in different places can be compared.
terms.example: Helmets for scooters in India must pass tests and carry the ISI mark.
terms.art: A scooter helmet with a small ISI mark sticker on the back.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that every material is made of. Atoms are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.
terms.example: A paper strip holds together because its atoms hold on to their neighbours with electric forces.
terms.art: A zoom from a paper strip to a fibre to a cluster of tiny balls holding hands.

explanations.definition: A fair test changes only one thing and keeps everything else the same. Then any difference in the result must come from the one thing you changed.
explanations.description: Imagine testing two cloths for an umbrella. You pour one spoon of water on the cotton, and five spoons on the plastic. More water comes through the plastic. Is plastic worse? You cannot tell, because two things changed: the cloth and the water. So a fair test asks three questions before you start. What will I change? What will I keep the same? What will I measure? In a materials test, you usually change the material. You keep the amount, the size, the time and the way you do it the same. You measure one result, with a number.
examples: Umbrella patch test: change the cloth. Keep the same rain, height, tumbler, patch size and waiting time. Measure the water that comes through.
Strength test: change the paper. Keep the same strip size and the same coins. Count the coins it holds before it tears.
Width test: this time change the width of the strip, and keep the paper the same. A fair test can change anything, but only one thing at a time.
explanations.art: A planning board with three columns, drawn as pictures: a hand swapping cloths (change), a padlock over a cup, spoon and timer (keep the same), and a measuring cup with a number (measure).
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: how to make a test of materials fair, so you can trust what it tells you.

explanations.definition: A results table is a grid. Each row is one thing you tested. Each column has a heading that says what was measured, and the unit it was measured in.
explanations.description: Scientists draw the table before they start testing. Then nothing gets forgotten. The first column lists the materials. The next columns hold the tries, for example Try 1, Try 2 and Try 3. The last column holds the middle value. Every heading needs its unit in brackets, like (cm) or (ml). A number with no unit means nothing. Is 12 a length in centimetres or a number of coins? A good table lets someone else read your results without asking you anything.
examples: Material | Try 1 (ml) | Try 2 (ml) | Try 3 (ml) | Middle value (ml)
Paper | Coins held, try 1 | Coins held, try 2 | Coins held, try 3 | Middle value (coins)
explanations.art: A hand-drawn results table on squared paper, with the units in brackets circled in red.
explanations.context: After a test you have lots of numbers. This card shows how scientists write them down so that anyone can understand them.

chart.title: A made-up example of a finished results table: the umbrella patch test

explanations.concept: Why we repeat a test three times
explanations.definition: One try can be a fluke. Repeating a test, and taking the middle value, gives a result you can trust more.
explanations.description: Small accidents happen in every test. A paper strip may have a tiny tear you did not see. A coin may be dropped instead of placed gently. So scientists repeat each test, usually three times. If the three results are close together, they are reliable. If one result is very different, it is called an odd result. Scientists do not just throw it away. They ask what went wrong, and they test again. To get one number for each material, put the three results in order and take the middle one. That is the middle value. An odd result cannot pull the middle value far off.
examples: A toilet paper strip held 14, 15 and 3 coins. In order: 3, 14, 15. The middle value is 14. The 3 is an odd result.
The woollen sweater let through 14, 15 and 6 ml in the umbrella patch test. The third square was cut from a tighter-knitted part of the sweater.
explanations.art: Three paper strips holding bags of coins, two holding full bags and one torn early at a tiny nick, circled with a magnifying glass.
explanations.context: Why not just test each material once? This card explains why scientists repeat their tests, and how they deal with a result that does not fit.

chart.title: Three tries with toilet paper strips (made-up results)
chart.note: Try 3 is an odd result. The strip had a tiny nick at its edge.

explanations.definition: A measured result is a number with a unit. Measuring turns 'this seems strong' into '14 coins', which anyone can check.
explanations.description: Saying 'the cotton got quite wet' is a start. But how wet? Your 'quite' might be my 'very'. A number is the same for everyone. That is why we measure water in millilitres, with a measuring cup. We measure length in centimetres, with a ruler. We measure weight by counting coins of the same kind. The tools must be the same for every material. Every coin in a test must be the same kind. A five-rupee coin is heavier than a one-rupee coin. Even one-rupee coins from different years can weigh different amounts. A number only helps if everyone measures in the same way. People have agreed on standard measures for thousands of years. About 4,500 years ago, the cities of the Indus Valley used bricks of the same shape everywhere. They also used stone weights of fixed sizes, so traders in different cities could trust each other.
examples: A medicine cup shows that 12 ml of rain came through the cotton hanky.
A ruler shows the strip is exactly 2 cm wide, not 'about two fingers'.
Indus Valley bricks were made in the same shape, about four units long, two wide and one thick.
explanations.art: A ruler, a medicine cup with millilitre lines, and a neat stack of identical one-rupee coins, beside an old Indus Valley brick and a little cube-shaped stone weight.
explanations.context: Words like 'strong' and 'quite wet' mean different things to different people. This card explains why scientists turn them into numbers.

explanations.concept: Why some materials keep water out
explanations.definition: Rain comes through a cloth by the gaps between its threads, and the biggest gaps let it through first. A waterproof material has no gaps, and water does not soak into it.
explanations.description: Water is made of countless tiny particles called molecules. Water molecules hold on tightly to each other, and they also cling to cotton and wool fibres. Every woven or knitted cloth has gaps between its threads. Where the gaps are big, the water simply falls through. Where they are tiny and the threads are packed tight, the water has to creep slowly along the fibres. So thickness is not what matters most. A thick sweater is knitted in loops, with big holes between them. Old jeans are woven tight, so their gaps are tiny. Their thick cotton also soaks up much of the water before it gets through. Plastic, rubber and wax have no gaps at all. Water clings to them only weakly, so it pulls itself into drops and sits on top. An umbrella is made of tightly woven cloth with a thin waterproof coating. But one pinhole is a gap, and the rain comes through there. In 1823, Charles Macintosh in Scotland found a way to seal rubber between two layers of cloth. Raincoats made this way are still called macs.
examples: Hold a cotton hanky and a piece of old jeans up to a window. You can see light through the hanky's gaps.
Rain makes round, rolling drops on a lotus or arbi (colocasia) leaf, and the leaf stays dry.
An old umbrella with one tiny hole drips in exactly one place.
explanations.art: A magnified view of three cloths side by side: a loose knitted sweater with big holes, a tight jeans weave with tiny gaps, and a smooth umbrella cloth with one pinhole and a drop under it.
explanations.context: In the umbrella patch test, some cloths let rain through and some keep it out, and thickness does not decide it. This card explains why, down to the tiniest bits of water.

explanations.concept: Why some materials soak up water
explanations.definition: Absorbent materials are full of tiny gaps between fibres. Water clings to the fibres and is pulled into the gaps. This pulling is called capillary action, or wicking.
explanations.description: Dip the bottom of a paper towel strip in water. Watch. The water climbs up, against gravity. It happens because water molecules cling to the fibres, and also hold on to each other. In a very narrow gap, the clinging pulls the water up, and the water drags more water behind it. The narrower and more numerous the gaps, the higher it can climb. Kitchen towels are made fluffy and loose on purpose, with many fine gaps. Printer paper is pressed flat and smooth, so it has fewer gaps, and water climbs it slowly. Capillary action also lifts water a little way up the thin tubes inside plants.
examples: Water climbs a kitchen towel strip much higher than a printer paper strip in 5 minutes.
A cotton wick in a diya pulls oil up to the flame.
Dip a sugar cube's corner in tea and watch the tea climb up.
explanations.art: A paper towel strip hanging in coloured water, the colour climbing up it, with a magnified circle of water creeping between fibres.
explanations.context: In the climbing water test, water creeps up some materials faster than others. This card explains the pull behind it.

explanations.concept: Why strips of the same paper tear at different numbers
explanations.definition: A strip tears at its weakest spot. Every strip has its own weak spots, so strips cut from the same sheet hold different loads. Scientists can say what usually happens, but not exactly what one strip will do.
explanations.description: Hold a paper napkin up to a window. Some patches are bright, where the fibres are thin. Some are darker, where they are thick. When you hang coins from a strip, the pull is shared across its whole width. But the strip does not wait for every part to give way. It starts to tear where it is weakest, and then the tear runs across. So a strip is only as strong as its worst spot. Each strip has a different worst spot, so the strips usually hold different numbers of coins. A bigger piece has more places, so it has more chances to hold a really bad spot. In 1939, a Swedish engineer named Waloddi Weibull worked out the maths of this. Engineers still use his maths to judge how far they can trust parts made of glass, ceramic or steel.
examples: For example, three 2 cm strips from one napkin might hold 18, 24 and 21 coins.
A hair with a knot in it broke at the knot, with fewer coins than a plain hair.
Climbing ropes are tested by breaking many sample pieces, because one piece tells you about only one piece.
explanations.art: A paper napkin held up to the light, its thin bright patches and thick dark patches showing, with three torn strips below it, each torn at a different thin patch.
explanations.context: In the width test, strips cut from the same napkin held different numbers of coins. This card explains why pieces of the same material are not all equally strong.

explanations.concept: Why things tear where there is a crack
explanations.definition: A tiny crack makes a material much weaker. The force of the pull crowds at the sharp tip of the crack, so the crack grows easily.
explanations.description: Try to tear a milk packet from its smooth top edge. It is hard. Now find the little notch that says 'tear here'. It rips easily. Here is why. When you pull a strip, the force is shared across its whole width. A crack leaves less material to share it. Worse, the force crowds together at the sharp tip of the crack. So the paper at the tip gives way first, then the next bit, then the next. That is how a small crack grows right across a strong strip. In 1913, a Cambridge engineer named Charles Inglis worked out how the force crowds around a hole. The sharper the end of the hole, the more it crowds there. In 1920, an English engineer named Alan Arnold Griffith tested thin glass threads. The thinnest were far stronger, for their size, than thick glass rods. His answer was that all glass has tiny hidden cracks, and a thin thread has room for fewer of them. This is why we check strips for tiny nicks before a strength test.
examples: A 'tear here' notch on a packet of biscuits or milk.
A paper strip with a tiny cut at its edge tears with fewer coins, and it tears from the cut.
Engineers drill a small round hole at the end of a crack in metal. A round end stops the pull from crowding at a sharp tip.
explanations.art: A milk packet with a 'tear here' notch, and a magnified view of a crack tip with many arrows crowding into its sharp point.
explanations.context: Why does a packet tear easily at its notch but not anywhere else? This card explains what cracks do to the strength of a material.

explanations.concept: Hard is not the same as strong
explanations.definition: Hardness is how well a material resists being scratched. Strength is how much pull or weight it takes before it breaks. A material can be very hard but break easily.
explanations.description: To test hardness, scientists use a scratch test. A harder material scratches a softer one, never the other way round. In 1812, a German scientist named Friedrich Mohs put ten minerals in order of hardness. Talc is the softest, and diamond is the hardest. Your fingernail can scratch chalk and soap. A metal key can scratch your fingernail. Most keys cannot scratch a window pane, so glass is harder still. But glass shatters if you drop it. It is hard, but it is brittle, which means it breaks without bending. Rubber is soft and easy to dent, but it is very hard to snap. So we need different tests for different properties.
examples: A fingernail scratches a bar of soap. Soap cannot scratch a fingernail.
A diamond can scratch glass. Glass cannot scratch a diamond.
A glass bangle is hard, but it breaks if dropped. A rubber band is soft, but hard to snap.
explanations.art: A ladder with ten rungs, from a soft chalky lump of talc at the bottom to a sparkling diamond at the top, and a fingernail, a key and a glass bangle placed beside the rungs they reach.
explanations.context: Is the hardest material also the strongest? This card explains the scratch test, and why hard and strong are different properties.

explanations.concept: Why things break after bending again and again
explanations.description: Bend a steel paper clip once. It does not break. Bend it back and forth twenty times, and it snaps. This is called fatigue. Aeroplanes, bridges and bicycle frames suffer from it too. Everyone agrees on the main story. Each bend makes tiny cracks a little longer, until one is long enough to snap. But exactly how the very first crack starts, deep inside, is still studied. And no one can yet predict the exact bend on which a particular clip will snap.
examples: A paper clip bent back and forth gets warm, then snaps.
A plastic ruler bent many times turns white at the bend before it cracks.

perspectives.explanation: Tiny cracks grow a little with every bend. We cannot see them, so we test many samples and give every part a big safety margin.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study atoms in metals
perspectives.explanation: Rows of atoms inside the metal slip a little with every bend. The slips pile up in bands, and the first cracks start where they pile up. How exactly this happens is still being worked out.

perspectives.who: Scientists who use chance and numbers
perspectives.explanation: Every clip has its own hidden flaws. So we can say how many clips will usually snap by 20 bends, but not which one.

explanations.art: A paper clip being bent back and forth by two fingers, with a magnified view of a tiny crack growing a little at each bend.
explanations.context: A paper clip does not break on the first bend, but it does on the twentieth. This card is about why, and about what scientists still argue over.

explanations.concept: Testing without breaking: the tap test
explanations.definition: Some tests break the thing you test, like pulling a strip until it tears. Other tests check a thing without harming it. These are called non-destructive tests.
explanations.description: You cannot test every bridge by breaking it. So engineers also check things gently. The oldest gentle test is tapping. A whole pot rings clearly when you tap it. A cracked pot sounds dull and buzzy, because the crack stops the pot vibrating as one piece. Potters have used this test for thousands of years. Many railways, in Britain and elsewhere, once had workers called wheel tappers. At stations, they walked along trains, tapping each wheel with a long hammer. A clear ring meant a sound wheel. Today, engineers send sound too high for us to hear into train rails and aeroplane parts. Echoes from inside show hidden cracks. Doctors use the same idea, ultrasound, to see a baby inside its mother.
examples: A potter taps a new pot with a knuckle and listens for a clear ring.
A coconut seller taps and shakes a coconut to judge how much water is inside.
Rail engineers check tracks for hidden cracks with machines that use ultrasound.
explanations.art: An old railway platform with a wheel tapper in uniform tapping a train wheel with a long hammer, and sound waves drawn coming from the wheel.
explanations.context: Some tests break the thing being tested. This card is about tests that check materials without harming them, from potters to railways.

explanations.concept: Why materials hold together at all
explanations.definition: Every material is made of atoms. Neighbouring atoms pull on each other with electric force. To tear or snap a material, you must pull those atoms apart.
explanations.description: Zoom into a paper strip, far past anything you can see. Paper is made of fibres. Each fibre is made of long chains of atoms. Neighbouring chains stick to each other, and fibres stick where they cross. When you hang coins on the strip, the pull spreads through all these links. A strip tears when enough links break at once. In steel, the atoms are packed in neat rows. Each holds tight to all its neighbours, so steel is very strong. In tissue paper, there are few fibres and few links, so it tears easily. Strength comes from how many of these tiny links there are, how tightly each one holds, and where links are missing.
examples: Wet paper is much weaker than dry paper. Water slips between the fibres and loosens their grip on each other.
A cotton thread is made of many short fibres twisted together. The twist makes them grip each other.
explanations.art: A zoom in four steps, from a paper strip holding coins, to tangled fibres, to one fibre made of long chains, to chains holding hands with little electric sparks between them.
explanations.context: Why does a paper strip hold coins at all, instead of falling apart? This card zooms deep inside a material to find out.

explanations.definition: Living things make materials that have been tested by survival over millions of years. Bone, spider silk, mother-of-pearl and tooth enamel are some of the best materials we know.
explanations.description: A spider's safety line, called dragline silk, is about as strong as steel for its thickness. But it is far lighter, and very stretchy too. Mother-of-pearl is the shiny inside of a seashell. It is made of tiny flat bricks of chalky material, glued with a soft protein. A crack in it cannot run straight. It has to wind around every brick, so the shell is very tough. Your bones are hard but slightly bendy, and they repair themselves when they crack. No factory can yet make spider silk as well as a spider does. Scientists test these materials, then try to copy them. Copying nature's designs is called biomimicry.
examples: A spider's web survives wind, rain and flying insects crashing into it.
The shiny inside of a seashell is mother-of-pearl. Find one on a beach in Goa or Puri.
A broken bone, held still in a plaster cast, mends itself in a few weeks.
explanations.art: A spider's web with dew drops, a seashell open to show its rainbow mother-of-pearl, and a close-up of the shell like a brick wall with a crack winding around the bricks.
explanations.context: People test materials in labs. This card is about materials that nature has been testing for millions of years, inside living things.

explanations.concept: The strongest material in the universe?
explanations.description: What is the strongest material of all? On Earth, the answer keeps changing as new materials are made. Graphene, a sheet of carbon just one atom thick, is one of the strongest ever measured. But the strongest material may be far out in space. When a giant star explodes, it can leave behind a neutron star. A neutron star is a ball only about as wide as a city, but heavier than our Sun. In its crust, scientists think matter is squeezed into strange shapes, like sheets and tubes of pasta. They call it nuclear pasta. In 2018, a team of scientists in the United States used computers to work out how strong it would be. They found it could be about ten billion times stronger than steel. Nobody can test it, because nobody can reach a neutron star. So this is an idea from calculations, not a measurement.
examples: Graphene can be made in a lab by peeling pencil graphite again and again with sticky tape.
The nearest neutron stars are so far away that their light takes hundreds of years to reach us.

perspectives.who: Matthew Caplan, Andre Schneider and Charles Horowitz, in 2018
perspectives.explanation: Computer models of nuclear pasta suggest it is the strongest material in the universe.
The models are a good start, but no one can test them directly. Watching neutron stars, and the ripples in space they make when they crash, may one day check the idea.

explanations.art: A tiny glowing neutron star beside a city skyline for size, with a magnified circle showing its crust shaped like lasagne sheets and spaghetti tubes.
explanations.context: This card follows the question 'what is strongest?' out into space, to a material nobody can ever test by hand.

agreed.text: A fair test changes only one thing and keeps everything else the same.
agreed.evidence: When two things change at once, nobody can tell which caused the result. Scientists all over the world plan tests this way, and so do children in classrooms.

agreed.text: Repeating a test gives results you can trust more than one try.
agreed.evidence: Repeated tries show whether a result was a fluke. Scientists publish how many times they repeated each test, so others can judge it.

agreed.text: Every material has a breaking point.
agreed.evidence: Testing machines have pulled strips of almost every material until they broke. Even steel and diamond break if the load is big enough.

agreed.text: A material gives way first at its weakest spot.
agreed.evidence: Paper strips tear where they are thinnest or nicked. Rain comes through a cloth at its biggest gaps. Engineers check welds, sharp corners and holes most carefully, because breaks usually start there.

agreed.text: Tiny cracks and flaws make materials much weaker.
agreed.evidence: Alan Arnold Griffith showed this with glass threads in 1920. Packets with a 'tear here' notch show it every day.

agreed.text: Things people trust with their lives are tested before they are used.
agreed.evidence: Helmets in India must pass tests to carry the ISI mark. In 1995, engineers bent the wings of a new Boeing 777 aeroplane until they snapped. They broke only at about one and a half times the biggest load the plane should ever meet.

challenging.claim: One test is enough to know which material is best.
challenging.who: A common way of thinking, especially when we are in a hurry
challenging.for: It saves time and materials. Sometimes the difference is so big that one try seems to show it clearly.
challenging.against: One try can be a fluke. A strip can have a hidden nick, or a coin can be dropped too hard. Repeating the test three times shows whether the result is real.
challenging.context: This card is about a common shortcut in testing: doing each test only once.

challenging.claim: If an advert says a product is the strongest, it must be true.
challenging.who: Many adverts on television and on packets
challenging.for: Companies do test their products. In India, false claims in adverts can be reported and stopped.
challenging.against: An advert does not show how the test was done, or what it was compared with. Was it fair? Was it repeated? A claim is only as good as the test behind it. David Kirkaldy, a Scottish engineer, ran a materials testing works in London from 1866. Over its door he put the words 'Facts not opinions'.
challenging.context: This card is about the claims we see in adverts, and how a fair test can check them.

challenging.claim: Every piece of the same material is equally strong.
challenging.who: A common idea, and the idea most engineers worked with until about 1920
challenging.for: Pieces from the same factory look the same, and their strengths are often close.
challenging.against: Every piece has its own hidden flaws, and it breaks at the worst one. Three strips from one napkin usually hold different numbers of coins. In 1920, Alan Arnold Griffith showed that hidden cracks set the strength of glass. In 1939, Waloddi Weibull worked out the maths of the spread.
challenging.context: This card is about whether 'the strength of steel' or 'the strength of paper' is one fixed number.

challenging.claim: If a material passes a test, it will behave the same way in real use.
challenging.who: A common hope, and the reason tests are made to copy real use
challenging.for: Good tests are designed to be like the real job, and they catch most problems. Helmets, ropes and wings are all tested this way.
challenging.against: A test answers only the question it asks. In the Second World War, some welded ships were built of steel that passed the usual tests. Those tests pulled smooth bars at room temperature. In icy seas, the same steel turned brittle, and cracks started at sharp corners. Constance Tipper, a scientist at Cambridge, showed why the steel turned brittle in the cold. A test for brittle steel, the Tipper test, is named after her.
challenging.context: This card is about the gap between a test and real life. A kitchen towel is used wet, and an umbrella meets wind as well as rain.

challenging.claim: A hard material is always a strong material.
challenging.for: Many hard things, like stone and steel, are also strong.
challenging.against: Glass is harder than a metal key in a scratch test, but it shatters when dropped. Rubber is soft, but very hard to snap. Hardness and strength are different properties, so they need different tests.
challenging.context: This card is about mixing up two different properties: being hard and being strong.

challenging.claim: Real testing only happens in big laboratories with expensive machines.
challenging.for: Big testing machines can pull a steel bar with a force far stronger than any person could.
challenging.against: Agnes Pockels was not allowed to go to university, because she was a woman. In the 1880s, she ran careful fair tests in her kitchen in Germany. Her results were printed in the famous science journal Nature in 1891. Many good tests need only care, patience and a table.
challenging.context: This card is about where real science happens, and who is allowed to do it.

big_questions.q: Why does a fair test change only one thing? What goes wrong if you change two?
big_questions.hint: Imagine you changed the cloth and the amount of water. More water came through. What caused it?

big_questions.q: Can you ever be completely sure a material will not break?
big_questions.hint: Engineers test many samples and then build things much stronger than they need. Why do you think they add extra?

big_questions.q: Why does water roll off a lotus leaf but soak into a cotton hanky?
big_questions.hint: Think about what water likes to cling to, and what the lotus leaf looks like close up.

big_questions.q: Is it fair to test every child with the same test, like we test every cloth with the same water?
big_questions.hint: A test is fair to materials when only the material changes. But children are different in many ways. What would a fair test of a person look like?

big_questions.q: Three strips cut from the same napkin held different numbers of coins. So what is 'the strength of paper'? Is it one number at all?
big_questions.hint: Think about the middle value. Is it the strength of any one strip, or something else?

big_questions.q: An advert says 'the strongest bag in India'. What would you need to know before you believed it?
big_questions.hint: Think of the three planning questions: what changed, what stayed the same, what was measured.

big_questions.q: Agnes Pockels did real science at her kitchen sink, but she was not allowed to go to university. How many good scientists might the world have missed?
big_questions.hint: Who is allowed to do science today? Who still finds it hard?

big_questions.q: Is it right to test something until it breaks?
big_questions.hint: Engineers break some wings and helmets so that others never break. Is breaking a few worth keeping many safe?

big_questions.q: Spiders make silk stronger than steel for its weight, at room temperature, from what they eat. Why can't our factories do that yet?
big_questions.hint: Think about how many millions of years spiders have been 'testing' their silk.

big_questions.q: Is a crack a thing, or a place where a thing is missing? Can something that is missing change what happens?
big_questions.hint: One pinhole let rain through a cloth that was waterproof everywhere else. What was at the pinhole?

big_questions.q: The strongest material might be inside a dead star that no one can ever touch. Can we really know something we can never test?
big_questions.hint: Scientists use calculations and watch the sky. Is that a kind of test too?

big_questions.q: Paper, rubber, steel and a lotus leaf are all made of atoms that hold on to each other with the same electric force. Are you and a tree made of different things, or of the same atoms held together in different ways?
big_questions.hint: Think of the strip test. What was really holding the paper together?

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, engineers thought each material had one fixed strength. Every rod of the same glass should break at about the same load. But there was a puzzle. Atoms hold their neighbours so tightly that glass should be many times stronger than any real piece. In 1913, Charles Inglis, an engineer at Cambridge, worked out that the force of a pull crowds around the end of a hole or crack. The sharper the end, the more it crowds. In 1920, Alan Arnold Griffith, an engineer at Farnborough in England, drew glass into thinner and thinner threads. The thinnest threads were many times stronger, for their size, than thick rods. He explained that real glass is full of tiny cracks, and it breaks at the worst one. A thin thread has room for fewer cracks. For years, few engineers used his idea. Then, in the Second World War, some welded American ships cracked, and a few broke in two. The cracks often began at sharp corners. Constance Tipper, a scientist at Cambridge, showed that this steel turned brittle in icy water, like glass. After the war, George Irwin and others turned these ideas into the science of cracks, called fracture mechanics.
how_we_found_out.who: Charles Inglis (1913), Alan Arnold Griffith (1920) and Constance Tipper (1940s)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That each material has one fixed strength, so every piece of the same glass or steel is about equally strong. Griffith's thin glass threads were far stronger for their size than thick rods. That showed that hidden cracks, not the material alone, set the breaking load.
how_we_found_out.art: An engineer in a 1920s laboratory drawing a glowing glass rod into a long, hair-thin thread over a small flame, a row of thick glass rods on the bench beside him.

story.title: The Button on the Water
story.note: Agnes Pockels (1862 to 1935) is real. She lived in Braunschweig, Germany. She could not go to university because she was a woman, and she looked after her ill parents. She tested the skin of water at home with a tray, a sliding tin strip and a small balance that lifted a button. Her brother Friedrich (Fritz) studied physics and sent her books. Her letter to Lord Rayleigh in January 1891 was printed in Nature in March 1891. She received an honorary doctorate in 1932, the year Irving Langmuir won the Nobel Prize for related work. The jumping numbers, the onions, the open window and her exact feelings are imagined.
text: In the town of Braunschweig, in Germany, about 140 years ago, there was a kitchen with a window that looked out on a grey street. In that kitchen, every evening, a young woman named Agnes Pockels washed the dishes.

Agnes was clever, and she loved science more than almost anything. But in Germany at that time, women were not allowed to study at a university. Her younger brother, Fritz, went away to study physics. Agnes stayed at home. Her mother and father were often ill, and somebody had to look after them. So Agnes cooked, and cleaned, and washed the dishes.
Fritz sent her his science books. She read them at night by the lamp, with her feet tucked under her.

And at the sink, she noticed things. When the washing-up water was clean, its surface seemed to hold together, like a skin stretched tight across a drum. When a little grease from the plates got into it, the skin went slack. A drop of soap made it slacker still. Nobody had asked her to notice this. It was only dishwater. But Agnes wondered. How strong is the skin of water? And could she measure it?

She built her own instrument from things in the house. She took a long, narrow tin tray and filled it to the brim with water. She laid a thin strip of tin across it, like a little wall that could slide. From one arm of a small balance, she hung a button. She lowered the button until it lay flat on the water. Then, very gently, she added tiny weights to the other side, until the button tore free with a small kiss of a sound. The weight it took told her how strongly the water's skin had held on. Scientists today call the pull of that skin surface tension.

The first evening, the button came free at one number. The second evening, at another. The third evening, at a different number again. She wrote every number in her notebook in neat columns, and the columns made no sense. She tried again. The numbers jumped about like sparrows on a roof.
Perhaps, she thought, I am not clever enough after all. Perhaps a kitchen is no place for science.

She sat at the table with the notebook open. The lamp hissed. In the next room, her father coughed. And slowly, she began to ask a different question. Not 'What is wrong with me?' but 'What is different each time?'

She made a list. On Monday, she had washed the tray with soap. On Tuesday, only with water. On Wednesday, she had touched the edge of the water with a finger, and her fingers had been peeling onions. Once, the window had been open, and dust had drifted in. The button was the same each time. The balance was the same. But the surface of the water was never the same. Without meaning to, she had changed many things at once. So how could she tell which one mattered?

The next evening, she began again. This time she was strict. She scrubbed the tray the same way, for the same time. She filled it with the same fresh water from the same jug. She kept her fingers out. She shut the window. Before each test, she slid the tin strip slowly along the tray, sweeping the surface clean, the way you sweep a doorstep before you draw a rangoli. Everything stayed the same, except the one thing she wanted to test.

The button came free. She wrote down the number. She swept the surface and tried again. The same number, or very nearly. And again. The same. Three numbers in a row, standing still at last, like sparrows settled on a wire.

Now she could begin. She added one tiny drop of oil, and measured. Then two drops. She tried soap, and then other things from the cupboard. Each time she changed one thing, and only one. She wrote the results in her table: what she added, how much, and the weight it took to lift the button. When she slid the tin strip to squeeze an oily surface into a smaller and smaller space, she found something strange. Nothing changed at all. Then, all at once, when the space was small enough, the skin's pull dropped away.
It was as if the oil were a crowd of people spread out over a big field. They only began to push against each other when the field became small enough.
For about ten years, Agnes kept testing and writing, in the evenings, after the dishes. Who would listen to a woman with no degree, who did her experiments next to the potatoes?

Then Fritz told her about a famous English scientist, Lord Rayleigh, who was studying the very same thing: thin films of oil on water. In January 1891, Agnes sat down and wrote him a long letter. She described her tray, her button, her sliding strip and her tables of numbers.

She expected nothing. But Lord Rayleigh read the letter carefully. He saw that her numbers were steady and her tests were fair. He sent her letter to Nature, one of the most famous science journals in the world. In March 1891, it was printed, with her name on it.

Years later, other scientists worked out what her squeezed oil films really were. They were layers of oil just one molecule thick. A woman at a kitchen sink had measured something far too thin for any microscope of her time to see.

In 1932, when Agnes was seventy years old, the university in Braunschweig gave her an honorary doctorate. That same year, an American scientist named Irving Langmuir won the Nobel Prize, for work that grew from a tray very like hers. Agnes never won a Nobel Prize. But her notebook is remembered. In its early pages, the numbers jump about. Then, on one page, they stand still.
story.epiphany: Agnes's numbers jump about because, without noticing, she changes many things at once: soap, onion fingers, dust. The turn comes when she stops blaming herself and asks 'what is different each time?' She keeps everything the same except one thing, and her repeated results agree. Only then can she test oil, soap and squeezing one at a time and write a meaningful table. That is a fair test and reliable, repeated results. The story also quietly asks who is allowed to do science, and who gets the prize.
ask: At first, Agnes's numbers kept jumping about. What was really causing that?
What did Agnes do to make every test the same? Name three things.
Why did her three numbers in a row matter so much to her?
Agnes was not allowed to go to university. Do you think that was fair? Who might still be kept out of science today?
Irving Langmuir won a Nobel Prize, and Agnes did not. How do you feel about that?

rules: Cut out the 24 test cards. Shuffle them and put them face down in a pile.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud.
Decide: is this test fair or unfair? Put the card on the FAIR mat or the UNFAIR mat.
If it is unfair, say what else changed, besides the material. A correct answer wins one token.
If you draw a FIX IT card, say how to make the test fair. A good fix wins two tokens.
When the cards run out, the player with the most tokens wins.

flow.do: 1. Lay the FAIR mat and the UNFAIR mat on the floor. 2. Shuffle the 24 test cards and put them face down. 3. Put the tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Every card is a test that a child did with materials. Our job is to be the judges. Was the test fair? A fair test changes only the material. Everything else stays the same.
flow.kid: Put down the two mats: FAIR and UNFAIR. Mix the cards and put them face down. Each card is a test. You are the judge!
flow.context: This is the first step of Fair or Unfair?, a card game about fair tests. A fair test changes only one thing, the material, and keeps everything else the same.

flow.do: Find the card about Arjun, who pours 1 spoon on the cotton and 3 spoons on the plastic. Play it together as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise. Arjun pours 1 spoon of water on the cotton and 3 spoons on the plastic. More water comes through the plastic. Is his test fair?
flow.kid: Practice card. Arjun pours 1 spoon on cotton. He pours 3 spoons on plastic. Is that fair? Tap your answer.

ask.q: What else changed, besides the material?
good: The amount of water.
He used more water on the plastic.

check.q: Arjun poured 1 spoon on the cotton and 3 spoons on the plastic. Is the test fair?
options: Fair, because he tested two materials
Unfair, because the amount of water changed too
check.why: Two things changed: the material and the amount of water. So we cannot tell whether the plastic let water through, or whether there was just more water. Picking 'fair' usually means thinking a test is fair as long as it compares materials. It must also keep everything else the same.

flow.do: 1. Take turns drawing a card and reading it out. 2. The player puts it on FAIR or UNFAIR. 3. For UNFAIR cards, they say what else changed. 4. Give one token for each correct answer.
flow.say: Read your card. Is it fair? If it isn't, tell us the sneaky thing that changed.
flow.kid: Take turns. Read your card. FAIR or UNFAIR? If it is unfair, say what else changed. Win a token!
flow.parent: Fair cards: Riya, Meena, Zoya, Sara, Tara, Asha, Leela, Ammu, Priya and Gita. The unfair cards, and the sneaky change in each: Arjun, the amount of water. Kabir, the strip width. Dev, the kind of coin. Imran, the time. Neel, the number of coins. Vikram, how deep the strip dips. Rohan, one try and picking results. Joseph, sun and shade. Sunny, how the coins are dropped. Ravi, where he measured from. Rohan's card is a good one to talk about. Keeping only the result you like is unfair to the truth.

flow.do: When a FIX IT card comes up, stop. Everyone says how they would make the test fair. The best fix wins two tokens.
flow.say: This test is broken. How would you fix it so that only the material changes?
flow.kid: A FIX IT card! How would you make this test fair? Say your fix out loud.

ask.q: How do you fix the test with a dry strip of tissue and a wet strip of kitchen towel?

Make both strips wet, the same amount.

flow.think: Is it possible to keep absolutely everything the same? What about the weather, or how tired your hands are?

flow.do: 1. Count the tokens to find the winner. 2. Look at the UNFAIR pile together and sort it by what changed.
flow.say: Look at the unfair pile. What sneaky changes come up most often? Amounts, times or sizes?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Who won? Look at the unfair pile. Which sneaky change came up most?
flow.think: Rohan kept only the result he liked. Is that worse than changing the water by mistake? Why?

printables.title: Fluke-finder sheet
items: Is there an odd result? Which one?

rules: Shuffle the result cards and put them face down.
Turn over a card. Everyone looks at the three tries.
The first player to say 'fluke!' and point at the odd result scores one point. If there is no odd result, the first to say 'reliable!' scores the point.
Then say what might have gone wrong in the odd try. A good reason scores one more point.
Last, everyone writes the middle value on their sheet. Each correct middle value scores one point.
After all 16 cards, the player with the most points wins.

flow.do: 1. Shuffle the 16 result cards and put them face down. 2. Give each player a fluke-finder sheet and a pencil.
flow.say: Each card shows a test done three times. Sometimes one try is very different from the others. Scientists call that an odd result. Let's be fluke-finders.
flow.kid: Each card shows three tries of one test. Is one try very different? That is a fluke. Be the first to spot it!
flow.context: This is the first step of Spot the Fluke. It is a game about repeated tests: finding results that do not fit, and the middle value of three tries.

flow.do: Turn over the card 'Toilet paper strip, coins held: 14, 15, 3'. Play it together as a practice round.
flow.say: Toilet paper strip, coins held: 14, 15 and 3. Which one is the fluke? What might have gone wrong? And what is the middle value?
flow.kid: Practice card: 14, 15 and 3 coins. Which try is the fluke? Tap it.

check.q: A toilet paper strip held 14, 15 and 3 coins. Which try is the odd result?
check.why: 14 and 15 are close together. 3 is far away from both, so it is the odd result. Maybe that strip had a tiny nick, or a coin was dropped too hard. Picking 14 or 15 usually means looking at the first or biggest number. Instead, ask which one does not fit with the others. The middle value is 14: in order, 3, 14, 15.

flow.do: 1. Turn over one card at a time. 2. The first to point at the fluke, or say 'reliable', scores a point. 3. Everyone gives a reason and writes the middle value.
flow.say: Fluke or reliable? Then tell me what might have gone wrong, and write the middle value.
flow.kid: Turn a card. Fluke or reliable? Say what went wrong. Write the middle value.
flow.parent: Flukes: toilet paper strip 3, kitchen towel 2, wool square 22, raincoat cloth 9, old band 22, newspaper climb 1, the second hair 20. The rest are reliable. To find the middle value, put the three numbers in order and take the middle one. For example, 9, 2, 10 becomes 2, 9, 10, so the middle value is 9. Good reasons include a tiny tear, a strip not touching the water, or a coin thrown in. Others are a cloth not stretched tight, a worn-out old band, or a gap at the edge of the cup.

flow.do: Add up the points. Then look at the cards with no fluke together.
flow.say: Look at the plastic bag card: 0, 0 and 0. Is that boring, or is it exciting?
flow.kid: Count your points. Who won? Plastic let through 0, 0 and 0. What does that tell you?
flow.think: If you only tested once and got the fluke, what wrong idea might you have believed?

items.p: What makes a test fair?
opts: You change only one thing and keep everything else the same
You use the biggest amount of water you can
You do the test very quickly
items.why: In a fair test, only the thing you are testing changes. Then you know it caused the difference. Picking 'lots of materials' usually means thinking more is better. But a test with many materials can still be unfair if the water or time changes too.

items.p: In the umbrella test, what is the thing we change?
items.why: We change the material, because we want to know which material is best. Picking 'the amount of water' is a common mix-up between what we change and what we measure. The water poured in stays the same. The water that comes through is what we measure.
items.context: This question is about the umbrella patch test. You stretch squares of old cloth over steel tumblers, let 20 ml of 'rain' drip onto each one, and after 4 minutes measure how much water came through.

items.p: In the umbrella test, sort these. Do we keep it the same, or is it the thing we measure?
items: the amount of water poured on
the size of the material square
the height the rain falls from
items.why: Everything is kept the same except the material. The one thing we measure is how much water came through.
items.context: This question is about the umbrella patch test. You stretch squares of old cloth over steel tumblers, let 20 ml of 'rain' drip onto each one, and after 4 minutes measure how much water came through.

items.p: Look at the chart. Which cloth would make the best umbrella patch?
items.why: Only 3 ml came through the old jeans, the least of the four. Picking the woollen sweater usually means the tallest bar was read as the best, or that thick was taken to mean waterproof. Here the bars show water that got through, so the shortest bar is best.
