chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your cloths are different, so your results will be too.

items.p: A material that does not let water through is called ____.
items.why: Plastic, rubber and wax are waterproof. Water cannot get through them.

items.p: A material that soaks up water and holds it is called ____.
items.why: Kitchen towels, sponges and cotton are absorbent.

items.p: Why do we test each material three times?
opts: Because three is a lucky number
Because one try can be a fluke
items.why: Accidents happen. A strip may have a hidden tear. Repeating shows if a result was a fluke. Picking 'the teacher says so' misses the reason, which matters more than the rule.

items.p: A paper strip held 9, 15 and 14 coins. What is the middle value?
items.why: Put them in order: 9, 14, 15. The middle one is 14. Picking 15 usually means taking the biggest. Picking 38 means adding them up, which gives the total, not the middle value.
items.context: This question is about the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a paper strip and add one-rupee coins, one at a time, until the strip tears.

items.p: Every heading in a results table should say its unit, like (cm) or (ml).
items.why: True. A number with no unit can be misread. Is 12 a length in cm or a number of coins? The unit tells us.

items.p: Match each test to the tool you use to measure it.
pairs: How much water came through a cloth
a measuring cup with ml marks
How long a rubber band stretched
How much weight a strip held
counting coins of the same kind
How high water climbed a strip
items.why: Each test needs a measuring tool, so the result is a number with a unit.

items.p: Dev used one-rupee coins for the first bag and five-rupee coins for the second. Why is that unfair?
opts: The coins are not the same weight
It is fair, because he still counted
items.why: A five-rupee coin is heavier than a one-rupee coin. So 10 coins of each are not the same weight. Picking 'it is fair' usually means thinking counting is enough. What we count must also be the same each time.
items.context: This question is about the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a paper strip and add one-rupee coins, one at a time, until the strip tears.

items.p: If you change two things at once, you can still tell which one caused the result.
items.why: False. If two things change, either one could have caused the difference. That is why a fair test changes only one.

items.p: Put the steps of a fair test in order.
items: Plan what to change, keep the same and measure
Write the results in a table
Say what you found and why
items.a: First plan what to change, keep the same and measure. Then make a prediction. Then do the test three times. Then write the results in a table. Last, say what you found and why. Planning and predicting can swap.
items.why: You plan first, so the test is fair. You predict before testing, so you can't change your guess afterwards. You record as you go, and explain at the end.

items.p: You want to find out which cloth would make the best school bag cover for the monsoon. Write what you would change, what you would keep the same and what you would measure.
items.a: Change: the cloth, for example cotton, plastic, jute and raincoat cloth. Keep the same: the size of each square, the amount of water, the cup and the time. Measure: how many millilitres of water came through in 1 minute.
items.why: A good plan names all three parts. Only the cloth changes.

items.p: Your toilet paper strip held 14, 15 and 3 coins. What would you do about the 3? Explain why.
items.a: The 3 is an odd result. I would check the strip for a tiny tear and do that try again with a fresh strip. Then I would use the middle value.
items.why: Scientists don't just ignore an odd result. They ask what went wrong and test again.
items.context: This question is about the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a paper strip and add one-rupee coins, one at a time, until the strip tears.

items.p: Draw an empty results table for the width test. It tests three strips 2 cm wide and three strips 4 cm wide. Give each column a heading with a unit.
items.a: Columns: Strip, Try 1 (coins), Try 2 (coins), Try 3 (coins), Middle value (coins), Where it tore. Two rows: 2 cm wide and 4 cm wide.
items.why: A table has one row for each thing tested, and a heading with a unit for each column.
items.context: This question is about the width test. You cut strips from one paper napkin, some 2 cm wide and some 4 cm wide, hang a bag from each, and add one-rupee coins until it tears.
items.art: A blank grid with six columns and three rows, the top row left empty for headings.

items.p: Look at the chart. Which paper made the strongest strip?
items.why: Kitchen towel held 60 coins, the most. It is made thicker, with more fibres gripping each other, so it does not fall apart when you wipe. Picking facial tissue usually means soft was mistaken for strong.
items.context: This question is about the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a paper strip and add one-rupee coins, one at a time, until the strip tears.

chart.title: Strip strength test: coins held by strips 2 cm wide before tearing (made-up middle values)

items.p: Kitchen towel held 60 coins and toilet paper held 15 coins. Kitchen towel held ____ times as many coins.
items.why: 60 divided by 15 is 4. Check: 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 60. So the kitchen towel strip held 4 times as many coins.
items.context: This question is about the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a paper strip and add one-rupee coins, one at a time, until the strip tears.

chart.title: Strip strength test: coins held by strips 2 cm wide before tearing (made-up middle values)

items.p: Look at the climbing water chart. Which of these would you choose to wipe up spilt water?
items.why: Water climbed highest up the kitchen towel strip, 9 cm, so it soaks up water fastest. Picking printer paper often means smooth and clean-looking was taken as good. Smooth paper has fewer gaps, so water climbs it slowly.
items.context: This question is about the climbing water test. You hang strips of different materials with their ends in coloured water, and after 5 minutes measure how high the water climbed.

chart.title: Climbing water test: how high the water climbed in 5 minutes (made-up middle values)

items.p: In the width test, 2 cm strips held 20, 24 and 22 coins. What is the best guess for a 4 cm strip of the same napkin?
items.why: The middle value for 2 cm is 22. Twice as wide means about twice as many fibres share the pull, so about 22 + 22 = 44. Real strips rarely give exactly 44, because each has its own weak spots. Picking 22 means thinking width makes no difference.
items.context: This question is about the width test. You cut strips from one paper napkin, some 2 cm wide and some 4 cm wide, hang a bag from each, and add one-rupee coins until it tears.

items.p: If you keep adding coins, a rubber band will keep stretching by the same amount for ever.
items.why: False. Every material has a limit. Near it, the band stretches less for each coin, and then it snaps at its weakest spot.
items.context: Think of a rubber band with a little bag hanging from it, and coins being added to the bag.

items.p: Why does water roll off a lotus leaf in round drops?
opts: The leaf has tiny waxy bumps, so water touches only their tips
Lotus leaves are made of plastic
The water is too cold to soak in
items.why: Tiny bumps covered in wax mean a drop touches almost nothing. Water clings to itself, makes a ball and rolls off. Picking 'hot' is a guess with no evidence. A cold lotus leaf in the morning does the same.

items.p: Why does a packet tear easily at its 'tear here' notch?
opts: The notch is made of weaker plastic
The pull gathers at the sharp tip of the notch, so it tears from there
It is a trick, it doesn't really help
items.why: A notch is a tiny crack on purpose. All the pull crowds at its tip, so the tear starts there. Picking 'weaker plastic' is a sensible guess. But the whole packet is made of the same plastic. Only the shape is different.

items.p: Sort these tests. Does the test break the thing, or leave it whole?
items: adding coins until a strip tears
bending a paper clip until it snaps
bending an aeroplane wing until it snaps
items.why: Tests that leave things whole are called non-destructive tests. They let us check the very thing we are going to use.

items.p: Match each person to what they did.
pairs: showed in 1920 that hidden cracks make glass weak
ran careful fair tests on water's skin in her kitchen
put minerals in order of hardness by scratching, in 1812
showed why the steel of some wartime ships cracked in icy seas
items.why: All four made careful tests. Two of them were women who did it at a time when women were often kept out of science.
items.context: This question is about four people from the history of testing materials.

items.p: A fingernail can scratch chalk. A steel key can scratch the fingernail. Which is hardest?
items.why: A harder material scratches a softer one. The key scratches the nail, and the nail scratches the chalk. So the key is hardest. Picking chalk usually comes from thinking that whatever gets scratched is the strong one.

items.p: Glass is very hard, so it never breaks.
items.why: False. Glass is harder than a metal key in a scratch test, but it is brittle. It shatters when dropped. Hard and strong are different properties.

items.p: Wet paper tears much more easily than dry paper. Why?
opts: Water slips between the fibres and loosens their grip on each other
items.why: Paper holds together because its fibres grip each other. Water gets between them and weakens that grip. Picking 'water is heavy' is a sensible guess. But a few drops weigh almost nothing, and the paper still goes weak.

items.p: Kabir tested a toilet paper strip 2 cm wide and a kitchen towel strip 4 cm wide. He says kitchen towel is stronger. What is wrong with his test? How would you fix it?
items.a: Two things changed: the paper and the width of the strip. A wider strip may be stronger just because it is wider. I would cut both strips the same size, 2 cm wide and 15 cm long.
items.why: To be fair, only the paper should change.
items.context: This question is about the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a paper strip and add one-rupee coins, one at a time, until the strip tears.

items.p: The umbrella cloth let 0 ml of water through. Does that mean it would make a perfect umbrella patch? What else would you want to test?
items.a: No. It keeps rain out when it is new, but a patch must also be strong in the wind and keep working after folding many times. I would test a strip of it with coins, and test it again after folding it 20 times. I would also check it for pinholes against the light.
items.why: One test checks one property. A real job usually needs several properties.
items.context: This question is about the umbrella patch test. You stretch squares of old cloth over steel tumblers, let 20 ml of 'rain' drip onto each one, and after 4 minutes measure how much water came through.

items.p: Write one sentence of each: what I think, what I saw, and why. Use the climbing water test.
items.a: What I think: kitchen towel soaks up water best. What I saw: water climbed 9 cm up the kitchen towel but only 2 cm up the printer paper. Why: kitchen towel is fluffy, with many tiny gaps between its fibres, so water is pulled up them.
items.why: This is claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good.
items.context: This question is about the climbing water test. You hang strips of different materials with their ends in coloured water, and after 5 minutes measure how high the water climbed.

chart.title: Climbing water test: how high the water climbed in 5 minutes (made-up middle values)

items.p: Draw what you think the edge of a torn kitchen towel looks like under a magnifying glass. Then draw the edge of torn printer paper.
items.a: The kitchen towel edge is fluffy, with loose fibres and big gaps. The printer paper edge is neater, with fibres pressed tightly together and few gaps.
items.why: The gaps between fibres are what let water climb.
items.art: Two empty circles side by side, like two views through a magnifying glass.

items.p: Neel tests a thin rubber band with 10 coins and a thick band with 20 coins. The thick band stretched more. He says thick bands are stretchier. What is the best reply?
opts: He is right, because the thick band stretched more
His test is unfair, because the number of coins changed too
He should have used paper money
Thick bands are always less stretchy, so he made a mistake reading the ruler
items.why: Two things changed: the band and the load. The thick band might have stretched more only because it had twice the coins. Picking 'thick bands are always less stretchy' jumps to a new rule without a fair test. We do not know until we test both with the same coins.
items.context: Neel hangs a bag of coins from rubber bands and measures how long each band gets with a ruler.

items.p: Vikram got 9, 2 and 10 cm for the kitchen towel. What should he say the middle value is?
items.why: In order: 2, 9, 10. The middle is 9. The 2 is an odd result, but it cannot pull the middle value far. Picking 7 means working out the average: 21 divided by 3. The average is pulled down a lot by the odd result, which is why the middle value is useful here.
items.context: This question is about the climbing water test. You hang strips of different materials with their ends in coloured water, and after 5 minutes measure how high the water climbed.

items.p: Agnes Pockels's numbers kept jumping about at first. Why?
opts: She was changing several things without noticing, like soap, dust and greasy fingers
She could not read numbers well
items.why: Many small things changed at once. Once she kept everything the same, her results agreed. Picking 'her balance was broken' is a common guess when results look messy. But the balance was the same each time. The surface of the water was not.
items.context: This unit's story is about Agnes Pockels. About 140 years ago, in Germany, she tested the skin of water in her kitchen, by lifting a button off the water with a small balance.

items.p: A knot in a hair makes it stronger, because there is more hair in the knot.
items.why: False. A knot bends the hair sharply round itself, and the pull crowds at the bends. The knotted hair breaks at the knot, with fewer coins than a plain hair.
items.context: In the Knot Test, you hang a little cup of one-rupee coins from plain hairs and knotted hairs, and count the coins until each one snaps.

items.p: Thin glass threads are much stronger, for their size, than thick glass rods. Why?
opts: Thin threads have fewer hidden cracks
Thin threads are made of a different glass
Thick rods are heavier, so they pull themselves apart
items.why: Alan Arnold Griffith showed in 1920 that hidden cracks make materials weak. A thin thread has less room for cracks. Picking 'heavier' is a sensible guess, but a short glass rod is not heavy enough to pull itself apart.

items.p: A paper clip bent once doesn't break. Bent twenty times, it snaps. What is this called?
items.why: Fatigue is when tiny cracks grow a little with every bend, until one snaps. Picking friction is a common mix-up, because the clip gets warm. The warmth comes from bending the metal, not from rubbing.
items.context: In the tap and bend activity, a grown-up bends a paper clip back and forth and counts the bends until it snaps.

items.p: An advert says 'Super Towel soaks up twice as much as other towels!' Plan a fair test to check it. Say what you change, keep the same and measure.
items.a: Change: the towel brand. Keep the same: the size of each sheet, the amount of water, the plate, the time, and the way I squeeze it. Measure: how many millilitres of water each sheet soaks up, by measuring what is left on the plate. Repeat each three times and compare middle values.
items.why: A claim is only as good as the test behind it. A fair test can check it.
items.context: In the kitchen towel project, you test real kitchen towels to see which soaks up most, and which is the best buy.

items.p: Helmets are tested by dropping them, until some crack. Is it right to break things in a test? Give one reason for and one against.
items.a: For: breaking a few helmets in tests means the helmets people wear won't break in an accident. Against: it uses up materials and money, and the broken ones are wasted. Overall, testing things that keep people safe is worth it.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A good answer gives a reason for each side.

items.p: Which of these can we NOT test directly, so scientists use computer calculations instead?
opts: How strong nuclear pasta inside a neutron star is
How strong a paper strip is
How stretchy a rubber band is
items.why: Nobody can reach a neutron star, so its strength comes from calculations. Picking any other answer misses that we can test those at home today.

items.p: Why do engineers build bridges much stronger than they need to be?
opts: Every piece of material has hidden flaws, and loads can be bigger than expected
Because the law says bridges must be heavy
items.why: Tests show that pieces of the same material vary in strength, and that cracks can grow over time. So engineers add a big safety margin. Picking 'cheaper' is wrong: extra strength costs more material and more money.

items.p: Spider silk is about as strong as steel for its thickness, but much lighter and stretchier. Imagine you could make lots of it. What would you make, and how would you test it first?
items.a: For example: a rope for rescuing climbers. I would test strips of it with coins or weights until they break, three times each, and compare with nylon rope of the same thickness.
items.why: A good answer names a use and a fair test that compares it with something we already use.

items.p: Put these in order from softest to hardest, using the scratch test: steel key, chalk, diamond, fingernail.
items.why: Each one scratches the one before it. A fingernail scratches chalk, a key scratches a fingernail, and a diamond scratches a key.
items.context: In a scratch test, a harder material always scratches a softer one, never the other way round. So you can put materials in order of hardness.

items.p: David Kirkaldy carved the words 'Facts not opinions' over the door of his testing works in London. What do you think he meant? Do you agree?
items.a: He meant that what a test shows counts more than what someone believes or says. I agree, but I think opinions are still useful for deciding what to test.
items.why: A thoughtful answer explains the motto and gives a view with a reason.
items.context: David Kirkaldy tested materials for a living in London, from 1866. He built a giant machine for pulling metal bars until they broke.

items.p: Why might Agnes Pockels's work have been nearly forgotten?
opts: She was a woman with no university degree, so few scientists took her seriously at first
She kept it all secret on purpose
Science did not use numbers then
items.why: Her results were careful and correct. Lord Rayleigh saw that, and sent her letter to Nature. Picking 'her results were wrong' is a common guess when someone is less famous. Fame and being right are not the same thing.
items.context: Agnes Pockels did careful tests in her kitchen in Germany in the 1880s. Women were not allowed to study at university there.

items.p: Invent a test for a property we did not test in this unit, like how well a material keeps heat in, or how bendy it is. Say what you would change, keep the same and measure.
items.a: For example: keeping heat in. Change: the material wrapped around a steel cup of warm water, such as wool, foil and newspaper. Keep the same: the amount and starting warmth of the water, the cup and the time. Measure: the warmth of the water after 20 minutes, with a thermometer.
items.why: A good answer has all three parts and a measuring tool.

items.p: Can a test ever be completely fair? Think about the weather, tired hands and tiny flaws in each strip. What can scientists do about this?
items.a: Not completely. There are always tiny differences. Scientists keep as much the same as they can, repeat each test, use the middle value, and tell others exactly how they did it so others can try it too.
items.why: This is a deep question. Good answers notice that repeating and sharing methods make tests trustworthy even when they cannot be perfect.

experiments.title: The Umbrella Patch Test: which cloth keeps the rain out?
experiments.question: Your umbrella has a tear. Which of four old cloths at home would make the best patch, letting the least rain through?
experiments.predict: Feel each cloth and hold it up to the light. Put the four in a line, from the one you think will let the least rain through to the one that will let the most through. Then say why you put your first one first. What did you notice that made you choose it?
experiments.fair_test: You plan this yourself, before testing. A fair plan changes only the cloth. It keeps the patch size, the tumbler and how tight the patch is the same. It also keeps the amount of rain (20 ml) and the height it falls from (10 cm) the same. Every patch waits 4 minutes from the start of its rain. The plan measures the water that comes through into the tumbler, in millilitres. Each cloth is tested three times, with a fresh dry patch and a dry tumbler each time.

materials.item: 4 kinds of cloth from old clothes, 3 squares of each, about 12 cm by 12 cm. For example: a cotton hanky or old kurta, old jeans, a polyester (synthetic) dupatta or sports T-shirt, and an old woollen sweater or shawl
4 steel tumblers of the same size
4 rubber bands
a small plastic water bottle with its cap, to be the rain bottle
a drawing pin, for a grown-up to make the holes
a medicine cup with millilitre marks (from a cough syrup bottle), or a measuring cup
a ruler
a timer or a phone
a tray or an old towel, to catch spills
a piece of old umbrella cloth or raincoat, or a square of plastic bag, for the last step
a magnifying glass, if you have one

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the holes in the bottle and the pinhole in the cloth, and cuts the old clothes. Use only clothes the family agrees can be cut. Work on a tray and wipe up spills straight away, so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Guess with a reason. Design the fair test. Test four cloths three times each. Find the middle values, try the pinhole, and write claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.record: Write your guess and your reason at the top. Fill in the results table: three tries for each cloth and the middle value. Draw a bar chart of the middle values. Then write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
experiments.context: This is the umbrella patch test. You design a fair test of four old cloths, let the same 'rain' drip onto each one over a steel tumbler, and measure how much water comes through. The least water through means the best umbrella patch.

flow.context: This is the first step of the umbrella patch test. Before any testing, you look closely at four cloths and make a guess, with a reason.
flow.do: 1. Lay one square of each cloth on the table. 2. Let your child feel each one, and hold each one up to a window. 3. Ask the question below. 4. Write down the order your child chooses, and their reason, word for word.
flow.say: Your umbrella has a tear, and we need a patch. Which of these four cloths would keep the rain out best? Put them in a line, best first. Why did you put that one first?
flow.kid: Feel each cloth. Hold each one up to the window. Which will keep rain out best? Put them in a line. Say why you chose your first one.

ask.q: Why did you put that one first?
good: It is the thickest.
I can't see any light through it.
It feels smooth and slippery, so water might slide off.
Wool keeps me warm, so it might keep water out too.

flow.parent: Don't say whether the guess is right, and don't give your own guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. The test will answer it. Thick does not always win, so many families are surprised.

flow.do: 1. Draw three boxes on a sheet of paper: CHANGE, KEEP THE SAME and MEASURE. 2. Ask your child to fill them in. 3. If something is missing, ask one of the questions in the note below. Let your child decide what to write.
flow.say: We want only the cloth to decide how much rain gets through. So what else could change if we are not careful? You plan the test. Fill in the three boxes.
flow.kid: Draw three boxes: CHANGE, KEEP THE SAME, MEASURE. You want only the cloth to make a difference. What else must stay the same?
flow.parent: Help only with questions. If the amount of rain is missing, ask: 'What if one patch got more rain?' If the height is missing, ask: 'What if we dropped the rain from higher on one?' If the time is missing, ask: 'What if one waited longer?' If tightness is missing, ask: 'What if one patch was loose and saggy?' A full plan: CHANGE the cloth. KEEP THE SAME the patch size, the tumblers, how tight, 20 ml of rain, 10 cm high and 4 minutes of waiting. MEASURE the millilitres that come through.

check.q: Riya rains on the cotton patch and lifts it after 1 minute. She lifts the wool patch after 4 minutes. More water came through the wool. Is her test fair?
options: Yes, because she tested two cloths
No, because the wool had longer to let water through
Yes, because she used the same rain
check.why: Two things changed: the cloth and the waiting time. The wool may have let more through only because it had three more minutes. Picking 'the same rain' notices one thing kept the same. But a fair test keeps everything the same except the cloth.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pushes a drawing pin through the bottle cap in 4 places, to make 4 small holes. 2. They make one more hole in the side, about 4 cm up from the bottom, to let air in. 3. Measure 20 ml of water in the medicine cup and pour it into the bottle. 4. Screw on the cap. 5. Keep a finger over the air hole. 6. Practise once over the medicine cup: turn the bottle upside down, hold it 10 cm up, and take your finger off. 7. Before the test, measure 20 ml into each of four small cups, so you can refill the bottle quickly.
flow.say: This is our rain bottle. Every patch gets the same 20 ml of rain, from the same height. Why do you think the air hole matters?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to make the rain bottle. Put 20 ml of water in it. Keep a finger on the air hole. Practise over the medicine cup.
flow.parent: With your finger on the air hole, the water stops, or nearly stops. Take it off and the rain falls in drops. Nearly all 20 ml should drip into the cup in under a minute. If it is slower, or water stays stuck in the bottle, make the holes a little bigger. Don't squeeze the bottle, because squeezing one more than another is a change. No bottle? Drip the 20 ml from a teaspoon, 4 spoonfuls, from 10 cm.

flow.do: 1. Stretch one square of each cloth over a dry tumbler. 2. Hold each with a rubber band. 3. Press a gentle dip in the middle with two fingers, about 1 cm deep, the same for each. 4. Put a paper label by each tumbler with the cloth's name.
flow.say: Every patch must be stretched the same way, with the same dip. Feel them. Are they all equally tight?
flow.kid: Stretch a patch over each tumbler. Hold it with a rubber band. Press a small dip in the middle. Label each tumbler.
flow.parent: A dip of about 1 cm holds about 20 ml. That is why we use 20 ml. More would spill over the edge.

flow.do: 1. Start the timer. 2. At minute 0, rain on tumbler 1. At minute 1, tumbler 2. At minute 2, tumbler 3. At minute 3, tumbler 4. 3. At minute 4, lift patch 1 by its edges. Tip any water on top into the tray. 4. Pour the water in tumbler 1 into the medicine cup. Read it at eye level and write it down. 5. Do the same for patch 2 at minute 5, patch 3 at minute 6 and patch 4 at minute 7.
flow.say: While we wait, look under the patches. Where do the drops come through? Everywhere, or in some spots?
flow.kid: Rain on one tumbler each minute. Lift each patch 4 minutes after its rain. Pour the water into the medicine cup. Read it. Write it down.

ask.q: Where did the drops come through first?
good: Through the middle of the dip.
Through one spot where the threads looked loose.
Through the holes between the wool loops.

flow.parent: The one-minute steps mean every patch waits exactly 4 minutes after its own rain. If your bottle takes longer than a minute, use two-minute steps. Rain at minutes 0, 2, 4 and 6, and lift each patch 5 minutes after its rain. Every patch still waits the same time, and that is what keeps it fair. Ask your child to bend down so their eyes are level with the water when they read the cup. Reading from above gives a wrong number.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: 1. Dry the tumblers. 2. Put fresh, dry squares on them. 3. Refill the rain bottle with 20 ml for each tumbler. 4. Do round 2 the same way. 5. Then do round 3.
flow.say: Same plan, fresh patches. Why do you think we need fresh, dry patches each time?
flow.kid: Dry the tumblers. Put on fresh patches. Do it all again, twice more. Same rain, same height, same waiting.

check.q: The woollen sweater let through 14, 15 and 6 ml. What is the best thing to do about the 6?
options: Use the 6, because it is the smallest
Ask what was different in that try, and use the middle value, 14
Add all three together
check.why: The 6 is an odd result. Perhaps that square was cut from a part where the knitting was tighter, or the patch was stretched more. In order the tries are 6, 14, 15, so the middle value is 14. One odd try cannot pull it far. Picking 'add them together' gives a total, which is not the result for one patch.

flow.parent: If the three tries for one cloth are far apart, look for the cause. A loose patch, a splash over the edge or a missed drop can do it. Fix it and do one more try. If two cloths give almost the same numbers, this test cannot tell them apart. Say so. That is an honest result too.

flow.do: 1. For each cloth, put its three numbers in order and take the middle one. 2. Draw a bar chart, one bar for each cloth. 3. Compare it with the guess you wrote at the start.
flow.say: Look at your first guess. Was it right? What surprised you most?
flow.kid: Find each cloth's middle value. Draw a bar for each. Look at your guess. Was it right? What surprised you?

check.q: On the umbrella patch bar chart, which bar shows the best patch?
options: The tallest bar
The shortest bar
The middle bar
check.why: The bars show how much rain got through. The best patch lets the least through, so its bar is shortest. Picking the tallest bar usually means thinking 'taller is always better'. In this test, a tall bar means a wet head.

chart.title: Umbrella patch test: rain that came through in 4 minutes (made-up middle values)
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your cloths are different, so your results will be too.

flow.do: 1. Stretch the umbrella cloth, raincoat or plastic square over a dry tumbler. 2. Test it once with 20 ml of rain. 3. Then a grown-up makes one hole in a fresh square with the drawing pin. 4. Ask your child to guess, with a reason. 5. Test the square with the hole.
flow.say: This cloth let no rain through at all. Now it has one hole, smaller than a grain of rice. Will a lot of water come through, a little, or none? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Test the umbrella cloth. Did any rain come through? Now a grown-up makes one tiny hole. Guess first, and say why. Then test it.

ask.q: Where did the water come through?
good: Only at the hole.
Drops grew under the hole and fell.

flow.parent: Usually the square stays dry underneath except under the hole, where drops form. Often 1 to 3 ml come through. If nothing comes through, the hole may be too tiny for the water to push in. Make it a little bigger with the pin and test again. The cloth is still waterproof everywhere else. One missing spot decides where the rain gets in. Keep this in mind for the Roots card.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why. 2. Then look at the thickest cloth and the thinnest cloth through the magnifying glass, or against the window.
flow.say: Now write three sentences. First, what you think now. Second, what you saw that shows it. Third, why you think it happened. Then look closely at the cloths again. Do you see anything new?
flow.kid: Write three sentences. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened. Then look at the cloths with a magnifier. What do you see now?
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good, even if the guess was wrong. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: old jeans make the best patch of our four cloths. What I saw: only about 3 ml came through the jeans. About 14 ml came through the sweater, even though it is thick. Why: the jeans' threads are packed tight, so the gaps are tiny. The sweater is knitted in loops, with big holes between them. Water goes through the biggest gaps first.
flow.think: The thick sweater may have let more rain through than the thin dupatta. What might matter more than thickness?

experiments.title: The Strip Strength Test: which paper holds the most?
experiments.question: Which thin paper makes the strongest strip?
experiments.predict: Before you test, feel each paper. Put them in a line, from the one you think will hold the most coins to the one that will hold the fewest. Why did you put your first one first?
experiments.fair_test: Change only the paper. Keep everything else the same. Every strip is 2 cm wide and 15 cm long, and taped the same way. Use the same bag, and one-rupee coins of the same design, placed gently one at a time. One-rupee coins from different years weigh different amounts. Measure how many coins the strip holds before it tears. Test each paper three times. Check every strip for nicks before you start.

materials.item: toilet paper, a paper napkin, a facial tissue and a kitchen towel (enough for 3 strips of each)
scissors and a ruler
sticky tape
a small plastic bag or paper cup with a string handle
a paper clip, opened into a hook
about 70 coins of one kind, all the same size and design, for example all one-rupee coins (borrow from a piggy bank). Not enough coins? Use level spoonfuls of dry rice, poured in one at a time
a table and a heavy book

experiments.safety: Keep your feet away from under the bag. When the strip tears, the coins fall. A grown-up helps with the scissors.

schedule.what: Plan the test. Cut the strips. Test each paper three times. Fill in the table and draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Write the middle value for each paper. Draw a bar chart.

flow.do: 1. Draw three boxes on a sheet of paper. Label them CHANGE, KEEP THE SAME and MEASURE. 2. Fill them in together. CHANGE: the paper. KEEP THE SAME: the strip size, the tape, the bag, and one-rupee coins added gently one at a time. MEASURE: how many coins the strip holds before it tears.
flow.say: Before any test, scientists answer three questions. What will we change? What will we keep the same? What will we measure? Let's fill in our planning boxes.
flow.kid: Draw three boxes: CHANGE, KEEP THE SAME, MEASURE. What will you change? What stays the same? What will you measure?
flow.context: This is the first step of the strip strength test. You will hang a bag from a strip of paper and add coins until the strip tears.

flow.do: 1. Help your child measure and cut strips exactly 2 cm wide and 15 cm long. Mark them with a ruler and pencil first. 2. Cut 3 strips of each paper. 3. Look at every edge for nicks. Throw away any nicked strip.
flow.say: Every strip must be the same size, or the test is not fair. Check the edges. A tiny nick could make a strip tear early.
flow.kid: Measure strips 2 cm wide and 15 cm long. Ask a grown-up to help cut. Check each edge for tiny nicks.
flow.parent: Tissue and toilet paper tear while cutting, so go slowly. If your toilet paper is very thin, use two layers for every paper, so it stays fair.

flow.do: 1. Lay the top 3 cm of a strip on the table. Put a heavy book on it, so the strip hangs over the edge. 2. Fold the bottom 2 cm of the strip round the paper clip hook and tape it. 3. Hang the bag on the hook.
flow.say: The book holds the top. The bag hangs from the bottom. Now the strip is doing all the work.
flow.kid: Put the top of the strip under a heavy book. Let it hang over the table edge. Tape a paper clip hook to the bottom. Hang the bag on it.

flow.do: 1. Add one-rupee coins one at a time, placing each gently into the bag. 2. Count out loud. 3. When the strip tears, write down the last number before it tore. 4. Repeat three times for each paper.
flow.say: Gently, one coin at a time. If we drop a coin in hard, it pulls harder than its weight, and the test is not fair.
flow.kid: Place coins in the bag one at a time, gently. Count out loud. When it tears, write down the number. Do each paper three times.

check.q: A toilet paper strip held 14, 15 and 3 coins. What should you do?
options: Use the 3, because it was the last try
Check that strip for a nick, test again, and use the middle value
Add all three together
check.why: The 3 is an odd result. Something probably went wrong, like a hidden nick or a coin dropped hard. Scientists check what happened and test again. The middle value, 14, is not pulled far off by the odd result. Picking 'add them together' gives the total, which is not the same as a result for one strip.

flow.parent: Twelve strips and about 400 coins take time, so let your child place the coins while you hold the bag still. Gather the fallen coins into a bowl after each tear. If you are using rice, pour one level spoonful at a time and count the spoonfuls.

flow.do: Draw the bar chart of middle values, one bar for each paper.
flow.say: Which paper is the strongest? Was your line of guesses right?
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each paper. Which is strongest? Was your guess right?

flow.think: Facial tissue felt soft and kitchen towel felt rough. Does soft mean weak?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now write three sentences. First, what you think now. Second, what you saw that shows it. Third, why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Write three sentences. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: kitchen towel makes the strongest strip. What I saw: kitchen towel held about 60 coins, and toilet paper only about 15. Why: kitchen towel is thicker, with more fibres holding on to each other.

experiments.context: This is the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a strip of thin paper and add coins, one at a time, until the strip tears. You do this for four papers, three times each.

experiments.title: The Width Test: does a strip twice as wide hold twice as much?
experiments.question: Strips cut from the same paper napkin: does a 4 cm strip hold twice as many coins as a 2 cm strip? And do strips of the same size all hold the same?
experiments.predict: Guess first, and say why. If a 2 cm strip holds 20 coins, how many will a 4 cm strip hold? And will three 2 cm strips from the same napkin all hold exactly the same number? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: This time, the thing we change is not the paper. It is the width of the strip. Keep everything else the same: the same napkin, one layer, and strips 15 cm long. Tape them the same way, use the same bag, and place one-rupee coins gently, one at a time. Measure how many coins each strip holds before it tears. Test three strips of each width.

materials.item: one large paper napkin, separated into single layers (napkins have no perforations, which are weak lines)
a ruler, a pencil and scissors
sticky tape
a heavy book and a table
a small plastic bag with a paper clip opened into a hook
about 60 coins of one kind, all the same size and design, for example all one-rupee coins

experiments.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors. Keep your feet away from under the bag. When the strip tears, the coins fall.

schedule.what: Cut three 2 cm strips and three 4 cm strips from one napkin. Test each one with coins. Compare the middle values, and the spread.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table, with where each strip tore. Write the middle value for each width. Then write: did doubling the width double the coins?
experiments.context: This is the width test. You cut strips of two widths from one paper napkin, hang a bag from each, and add one-rupee coins until it tears. You find out whether twice as wide means twice as strong, and whether strips of the same size are all equally strong.

flow.context: This is the first step of the width test. You guess, with a reason, how much a wider strip of the same paper will hold.
flow.do: 1. Show your child one layer of the napkin. 2. Ask the two guesses below. 3. Write both guesses and the reasons down.
flow.say: If a strip 2 cm wide holds 20 coins, how many will a strip 4 cm wide hold? Why do you think so? And will three strips of the same size all hold the same?
flow.kid: A 2 cm strip holds 20 coins. Guess: how many will a 4 cm strip hold? Why? Will three same-size strips hold the same?

good: Twice as wide is twice as much paper, so 40 coins.
They will all be the same, because it is the same napkin.
Maybe not exactly, because one might have a weak bit.

flow.parent: Don't correct the guesses. Write them down. Many children say '40' and 'all the same'. The test will show whether that is right.

flow.do: 1. With a ruler and pencil, mark three strips 2 cm wide and three 4 cm wide. Make them all 15 cm long. 2. Cut them out slowly. 3. Check every edge for nicks.
flow.say: Here we change the width on purpose. What must we keep the same?
flow.kid: Mark three strips 2 cm wide. Mark three 4 cm wide. Make all of them 15 cm long. Ask a grown-up to help cut. Check for nicks.
flow.parent: Napkin paper tears easily while cutting, so go slowly. Cut all the strips in the same direction across the napkin, because paper is often stronger one way than the other.

flow.do: 1. Trap the top 3 cm of a strip under the heavy book at the table's edge. 2. Fold the bottom 2 cm round the paper clip hook and tape it. 3. Hang the bag. 4. Add coins gently, one at a time, counting out loud. 5. When it tears, write the number, and mark on a drawing where it tore. 6. Test all six strips.
flow.say: Gently, one coin at a time. Before each new strip, guess again: more or fewer than the last one?
flow.kid: Hang a strip. Add coins one at a time. Count out loud. When it tears, write the number. Mark where it tore. Test all six.

ask.q: Did each strip tear in the same place?
good: No, each tore somewhere different.
Some tore at the tape, some in the middle.

chart.title: Made-up example results from one napkin

flow.do: Look at the results together. Compare the 4 cm middle value with double the 2 cm middle value.
flow.say: Did twice as wide hold twice as many? And look at the three 2 cm strips. Same napkin, same size. Why do you think they held different numbers?
flow.kid: Did twice as wide hold twice as many? The 2 cm strips held different numbers. Why might that be?

check.q: Three 2 cm strips from one napkin held 18, 24 and 21 coins. Why were they different?
options: Each strip had its own hidden weak spots, and it tore at the weakest
The coins got heavier
One of them must have been a different paper
check.why: Paper is a tangle of fibres, thicker in some places and thinner in others. A strip tears where it is weakest, and every strip has different weak spots. Picking 'a different paper' is a fair worry, but all three came from one napkin. Picking 'heavier coins' is not possible, because the coins were the same.

flow.do: Ask your child to write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Now write three sentences. First, what you think now. Second, what you saw that shows it. Third, why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Write three sentences. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a strip twice as wide holds about twice as many coins, but not exactly. Strips of the same size are not all equally strong. What I saw: the 2 cm strips held 18, 24 and 21. The 4 cm strips held about 44, which is close to double 21. Why: twice as wide means twice as many fibres share the pull. But each strip tears at its own weakest spot, and those are different in every strip.
flow.think: If you tested a strip 100 cm wide, would it hold exactly 50 times as many coins as a 2 cm strip? What could go wrong?

experiments.title: The Climbing Water Test: which material soaks up water fastest?
experiments.question: Which material soaks up water fastest, so that water climbs highest up it in 5 minutes?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Put the four materials in order, from the one you think water will climb highest up, to the lowest. Say why you put your top one first.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the material. Keep everything else the same: strips 2 cm wide and 15 cm long, the same coloured water, each strip dipped exactly 1 cm in, all started at the same moment, and 5 minutes of waiting. Measure how high the colour climbs above the water, in centimetres. Test three strips of each material at once.

materials.item: 3 strips, 2 cm by 15 cm, each of kitchen towel, cotton cloth, newspaper and printer paper
a baking tray or wide dish
a few drops of food colouring or ink, to colour the water. No colour? Use plain water: the wet part of each strip looks darker
a long stick, broom handle or ruler, and two piles of books of the same height, one on each side of the tray
clothes pegs or paper clips
a ruler and a timer

experiments.safety: Food colouring and ink stain clothes and hands. Wear old clothes and work on newspaper.

schedule.what: Hang 12 strips over coloured water from a stick on two piles of books. Wait 5 minutes. Measure, find middle values and draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Write the middle value for each material. Draw a bar chart.

flow.do: 1. Draw three boxes on a sheet of paper. Label them CHANGE, KEEP THE SAME and MEASURE. 2. Fill them in together. CHANGE: the material. KEEP THE SAME: the strip size, the coloured water, how deep each dips, the start time and 5 minutes. MEASURE: how high the colour climbs, in centimetres.
flow.say: Before any test, scientists answer three questions. What will we change? What will we keep the same? What will we measure? Let's fill in our planning boxes.
flow.kid: Draw three boxes: CHANGE, KEEP THE SAME, MEASURE. What will you change? What stays the same? What will you measure?
flow.context: This is the first step of the climbing water test. You hang strips of different materials with their ends in coloured water, and see how high the water climbs.

flow.do: 1. Draw a pencil line 1 cm from the bottom of each strip. 2. Peg the 12 strips along the stick, so they hang down. 3. Rest the stick on the two piles of books, with the strips hanging into the empty tray. 4. Add or take away a thin book. Stop when each strip ends about 1 cm above the floor of the tray. 5. Lift the stick off. Pour water into the tray, about 2 cm deep, and stir in the colour.
flow.say: The water will reach each pencil line. Same depth for every strip keeps it fair. Why do you think the depth matters?
flow.kid: Draw a line 1 cm from the bottom of each strip. Peg the strips on the stick. Rest it on the books. Fix the height. Then pour in the coloured water.
flow.parent: If a strip curls or does not touch the water, that strip will give an odd result. Straighten it before the timer starts.

flow.do: 1. Lower the stick back onto the two piles. Every strip now dips to its pencil line at the same moment. 2. Start the timer for 5 minutes. 3. Watch the colour climb.
flow.say: All of them start at the same moment. Watch closely. Which one is winning the race?
flow.kid: Lower the stick onto the books. All the strips dip in at once. Start the timer. Watch the colour climb. Which is fastest?

ask.q: What is pulling the water up, against gravity?
good: The water clings to the fibres and climbs the tiny gaps.
The strip is sucking it up.

flow.parent: 'Sucking' is a fine first answer. You can add: water clings to the fibres and to itself, and that pulls it up the narrow gaps. Scientists call this capillary action, or wicking.

flow.do: 1. After 5 minutes, lift the stick out. 2. Lay the strips on newspaper. 3. Measure from the pencil line to the top of the colour on each strip. 4. Write each number in the table and find the middle values.
flow.say: Measure from the pencil line, not from the very bottom. The line is where the water started.
flow.kid: Lift the strips out. Measure from the pencil line to the top of the colour. Write each one down.

check.q: Kitchen towel strips gave 9, 2 and 10 cm. What is the middle value?
options: 2 cm
9 cm
21 cm
check.why: In order: 2, 9, 10. The middle one is 9. The 2 is an odd result, perhaps that strip didn't touch the water properly. Picking 21 means adding them up, which gives a total, not a middle value.

chart.title: Climbing water test: how high the water climbed in 5 minutes (made-up middle values)

flow.do: Tear the end of a kitchen towel strip and a printer paper strip. Look at both torn edges through a magnifying glass.
flow.say: Look at the torn edges. Which one is fluffy, with lots of gaps? Which is pressed flat?
flow.kid: Tear the end of two strips. Look with a magnifier. Which edge is fluffy? Which is flat?
flow.think: A diya wick is made of cotton. Why not printer paper?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now write three sentences. First, what you think now. Second, what you saw that shows it. Third, why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Write three sentences. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: kitchen towel soaks up water fastest. What I saw: in 5 minutes, the water climbed 9 cm up the kitchen towel. It climbed only 2 cm up the printer paper. Why: kitchen towel is fluffy, with lots of fine gaps between its fibres. The water is pulled up the gaps.

experiments.context: This is the climbing water test. You hang strips of four materials with their ends in coloured water, and after 5 minutes you measure how high the water has climbed up each strip.

activities.title: The Planning Board

materials.item: a sheet of paper, a pencil and 8 small slips of paper or sticky notes

schedule.what: Plan a fair test using the three planning boxes and sticky notes.

activities.record: Keep your finished planning board. Use it again for the umbrella patch test.

flow.do: 1. Draw three big boxes on the paper: CHANGE, KEEP THE SAME and MEASURE. 2. Read out the question: 'Which cloth would make the best monsoon bag cover?'
flow.say: Scientists plan before they test. We'll write each thing that could change in a test on its own slip. Then we decide which box each slip goes in.
flow.kid: Draw three boxes: CHANGE, KEEP THE SAME, MEASURE. Here is the question. Which cloth makes the best rain cover?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Planning Board. It is a way to plan a fair test before you do it, using three boxes and slips of paper.

flow.do: Write one thing on each of 8 slips. They are: the cloth, the amount of water, the size of the square, the time we wait. Then: the cup, how tight the cloth is, the water that comes through, and who pours. Your child places each slip in a box.
flow.say: Where does each slip go? Remember, only one slip can go in the CHANGE box.
flow.kid: Put each slip in a box. Only ONE slip goes in CHANGE. Only ONE goes in MEASURE. The rest stay the same.

check.q: Which slip belongs in the MEASURE box?
options: The cloth
The amount of water we pour
The water that comes through
check.why: We measure the result: the water that comes through. The cloth is what we change. The water we pour is kept the same. Picking 'the amount of water we pour' is a very common mix-up. One amount of water goes in, the same every time. A different amount comes out, and that is what we measure.

flow.do: Look at the KEEP THE SAME box together. Ask what would happen if one of those slips changed.
flow.say: What if we poured more water on the cotton than on the plastic? Could we still trust the result?
flow.kid: Pick one slip from KEEP THE SAME. What if it changed? Would the test still be fair?

ask.q: What if a different person poured the water each time?
good: They might pour faster or slower.
Better if the same person pours every time.

flow.do: Draw an empty results table below the boxes. The CHANGE slip names the rows. The MEASURE slip names the columns.
flow.say: The table comes straight from the plan. The things we change go down the side. What we measure goes across the top, with its unit.
flow.kid: Draw a table. Write the cloths down the side. Write 'Water through (ml)' across the top. Add Try 1, Try 2, Try 3.
flow.think: Could you plan a test for something at home, like which chappal grips best, or which soap makes most bubbles?

activities.title: The One Hair Test

materials.item: one long hair from each family member who agrees, each cut to about 20 cm
a pencil, sticky tape and a paper clip opened into a hook
a very light paper cup with a thread handle, or a tiny plastic bag
about 40 one-rupee coins, all of the same kind
a ruler and a heavy book

activities.safety: Only use hair that someone has agreed to give. Pull gently. Keep feet away from falling coins.

schedule.what: Test how many coins one hair can hold, for each family member.

activities.record: Make a table: whose hair, coins held on each try, middle value. Write one sentence about what surprised you.

flow.do: 1. Ask family members for one long hair each. 2. Cut each one to 20 cm, using the ruler. 3. Wind the top of the hair three times round a pencil and tape it there. 4. Put the pencil under a heavy book at the table's edge, so the hair hangs down. 5. Wind the bottom of the hair five times round the paper clip hook, then tie it and tape it. 6. Hang the cup on the hook.
flow.say: One single hair. How many coins do you think it can hold? Guess first, and tell me why.
flow.kid: Cut one hair to 20 cm. Wind the top round a pencil and tape it. Put the pencil under a book. Wind the bottom round the hook and tape it. Hang the cup. Guess: how many coins?
flow.context: This is the first step of the One Hair Test. You find out how many one-rupee coins a single hair can hold before it snaps.
flow.parent: The turns round the pencil and the hook take the pull, so the hair breaks along its length, not at a knot. A knot is a weak spot, as the Knot Test shows.

flow.do: 1. Add coins one at a time, gently. 2. Count until the hair snaps. 3. Write the number. 4. Repeat with a second and third hair from the same person if they agree. 5. Then test the other family members' hairs the same way.
flow.say: Gently, one at a time. What makes this test fair? What must be the same for every hair?
flow.kid: Add coins one at a time. Count until it snaps. Write it down. Test each person's hair the same way.
flow.parent: Many hairs hold between 10 and 25 one-rupee coins, which is roughly 30 to 120 grams, depending on the coins. If the hair slips off the pencil or the hook instead of snapping, that try is an odd result. Wind it again and repeat.

chart.title: Made-up example results: one hair, 20 cm long

flow.do: Work out how many coins the whole head of hair might hold together.
flow.say: A head has about one hundred thousand hairs. If each holds about 20 coins, together they could hold two million coins. That is about as heavy as two elephants. Of course, the scalp would let go long before that.
flow.kid: Your head has about 100,000 hairs. Together they could hold as much as two elephants! But your head would not like it.

check.q: Why must every hair be cut to the same length for a fair test?
options: Because long hair looks nicer
So that only the person's hair changes, not the length
Because short hair can't be tied
check.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. Here it is whose hair it is. If the lengths were different too, we could not tell which mattered. Picking 'short hair can't be tied' is a practical worry. But it is not why the test needs the same length.

flow.do: Talk together about what makes hair strong.
flow.say: Hair is made of a material called keratin. Your nails are made of it too, and so are a cow's horns. It is made of long chains twisted together, like a rope.
flow.kid: Hair is made of keratin, like your nails. Inside, it is like a tiny twisted rope.
flow.think: Grandmother's hair and your hair held different amounts. Is that because of age, or something else? How could you find out fairly?

activities.context: This activity tests how strong one single hair is. You hang a little cup of one-rupee coins from a hair and count until it snaps, comparing hairs from your family.

activities.title: The Muffle Test: which material absorbs sound best?

materials.item: a phone that can play a steady alarm sound, and a second phone with a free sound meter app (or a measuring tape instead)
a large steel bowl or a cardboard box to cover the alarm
covers to test: a towel, a woollen shawl, aluminium foil and two sheets of newspaper
a ruler or measuring tape

activities.safety: Keep the alarm at a gentle volume. Never hold a loud sound close to anyone's ear.

schedule.what: Measure how loud an alarm sounds under different covers, three times each.

activities.record: Fill in a table: cover, three readings, middle value. Draw a bar chart. Put the covers in order from best muffler to worst.

flow.do: 1. Set the alarm phone to ring with a steady sound at a gentle volume. 2. Put it on a table under the upturned bowl. 3. Put the second phone, with the sound meter app, on the table exactly 1 metre away. 4. Measure with no cover over the bowl. Write the number.
flow.say: A sound meter app shows a number for how loud a sound is. The unit is called the decibel. A bigger number means a louder sound. First we measure with no cover at all. Which cover do you think will hush it most? Why?
flow.kid: Put the alarm under the bowl. Put the sound meter phone 1 metre away. Read the number. A bigger number means louder.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Muffle Test. You cover a ringing alarm with different materials and measure how loud it still sounds, to find which material absorbs sound best.

flow.do: 1. Wrap the bowl in the first cover, one layer. 2. Start the alarm. 3. Read the sound meter after 5 seconds. 4. Write it down. 5. Do this three times for each cover.
flow.say: Same alarm, same volume, same bowl, same distance. Only the cover changes. What else must we keep the same?
flow.kid: Wrap the bowl in one cover. Start the alarm. Read the number. Do each cover three times.
flow.parent: No second phone? Then measure how far away you can walk before you stop hearing the alarm. Use a measuring tape. A shorter distance means a better muffler. Keep the room as quiet as you can, and switch off fans, because noise around you is a change too.

chart.title: Made-up example: how loud the alarm sounded under each cover (middle values)
chart.note: A lower bar means the cover absorbed more sound.

flow.do: Look at the results together and put the covers in order, best muffler first.
flow.say: Which cover absorbed the most sound? Was it the hard, shiny one, or a soft, fluffy one?
flow.kid: Which cover made the alarm quietest? Was it soft and fluffy, or hard and shiny?

check.q: Which kind of material usually absorbs sound best?
options: Hard, smooth materials like foil
Soft, fluffy materials with lots of air gaps, like wool
Shiny materials
check.why: Sound is a vibration, a fast shaking, that travels through the air. In wool and towels, the vibration gets lost in millions of tiny fibres and air gaps. It turns into a tiny bit of warmth. Hard, smooth foil bounces much of the sound back instead. We say soft materials absorb sound. Picking foil usually comes from thinking a metal wall must block more. Hard walls do block sound well when they are thick and heavy, but thin foil is not.

flow.do: Talk about where people use muffling materials.
flow.say: Recording studios and cinemas cover their walls with soft panels. Why do you think a room with carpets and curtains sounds quieter than an empty room?
flow.kid: Why do cinemas have soft walls? Why does an empty room echo?
flow.think: A towel hushed the alarm better than foil. Would two layers of towel hush it twice as much? How could you test it fairly?

activities.context: This activity tests which material absorbs sound best. You cover a ringing phone alarm with different materials and measure how loud it still is with a sound meter app.

activities.title: The Squash Test: which material springs back?

materials.item: things to squash: a kitchen sponge, a piece of packing foam, a pad of cotton wool, a slice of bread and a folded cloth
a square of cardboard, a little bigger than the sponge
three heavy books, the same three every time
a ruler
a timer

activities.safety: Lower the books gently. Keep fingers out from under them.

schedule.what: Squash five materials under the same books. Measure how thick they are before, during and after.

activities.record: Fill in a table: material, thickness before (cm), thickness under the books (cm), thickness 1 minute after (cm). Circle the ones that sprang back.

flow.do: 1. Stand the ruler upright beside the first material. 2. Measure how thick it is, in centimetres. 3. Write it down.
flow.say: First we measure how thick each thing is, before we squash it. Which ones do you think will spring back? Why?
flow.kid: Stand the ruler beside the sponge. How thick is it? Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Squash Test. You squash different materials under the same heavy books, and measure whether they spring back.

flow.do: 1. Put the cardboard square on top. 2. Gently lower the same three books on top. 3. Measure the thickness now. 4. Lift the books off. 5. Wait 1 minute, then measure again. 6. Do the same for each material.
flow.say: Same books, same cardboard, same minute of waiting. Only the material changes.
flow.kid: Put the card on top. Lower the three books gently. Measure. Lift them off. Wait 1 minute. Measure again.

chart.title: Made-up example results

flow.do: Sort the materials into two groups: sprang back, and stayed squashed.
flow.say: Look at your table. Which ones went back to their old thickness? Which stayed squashed? What do you think is different inside them?
flow.kid: Which ones sprang back? Which stayed squashed? What might be different inside them?

check.q: The bread was 2.5 cm, then 1 cm under the books, and still 1 cm a minute later. What does that show?
options: Bread is elastic, it springs back
Bread stays squashed: once its air holes collapse, they don't spring back
The ruler was wrong
check.why: The bread did not go back to 2.5 cm, so it stayed squashed. Its soft walls of baked dough crushed and stuck together. A sponge's walls are springy, so they push back open. Picking 'elastic' means looking at the squash, not at what happened after. Both squashed. Only one sprang back.

flow.think: A sponge, foam and bread are all full of air holes. Why does only one kind spring back? What would happen to a sponge squashed a thousand times?
flow.parent: After your child has answered, give the words. Springing back is called elastic. Staying squashed is called plastic, from an old Greek word that means 'can be shaped'.

activities.context: This activity tests how materials squash. You press five materials under the same three books, and measure whether each one springs back to its old thickness.

activities.title: The Knot Test: does a knot make a hair stronger or weaker?

materials.item: six long hairs from one person who agrees, each cut to 20 cm
a pencil, sticky tape, a heavy book and a paper clip opened into a hook
a very light paper cup with a thread handle, or a tiny plastic bag
about 40 one-rupee coins, all of the same kind
a ruler
a magnifying glass, if you have one

activities.safety: Only use hair that someone has agreed to give. Pull gently. Keep feet away from the falling coins.

schedule.what: Test three plain hairs and three knotted hairs from the same person. Count the coins each holds, and see where each one breaks.

activities.record: Make a table: plain or knotted, coins held on each try, middle value, and where it broke.
activities.context: This activity tests whether a knot makes a hair stronger or weaker. You hang a little cup of one-rupee coins from plain hairs and from knotted hairs, and count until each one snaps.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Knot Test. You guess, with a reason, what a knot will do to a hair's strength.
flow.do: 1. Show your child the six hairs. 2. Ask the question below. 3. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Three of these hairs will stay plain. Three will get a knot in the middle. Will the knotted ones hold more coins, fewer, or the same? Why do you think so? And where will a knotted hair break?
flow.kid: Three plain hairs. Three with a knot. Which will hold more coins? Why do you think so? Where will a knotted hair break?

good: More, because the knot is extra hair.
Fewer, because the knot bends the hair.
The same, because it is the same hair.

flow.parent: Don't say what you expect. Every guess with a reason is a good start.

flow.do: 1. Tie a simple knot in the middle of three hairs. Make a loop, pass one end through it and pull it gently tight. 2. Wind the top of a hair three times round a pencil and tape it. Put the pencil under the heavy book at the table's edge. 3. Wind the bottom five times round the paper clip hook, then tie it and tape it. 4. Hang the cup on the hook.
flow.say: Every hair is from the same person, the same length, hung the same way. What is the one thing that changes?
flow.kid: Tie a knot in three hairs. Wind the top round a pencil, under the book. Wind the bottom round the hook. Hang the cup.
flow.parent: The turns at the pencil and the hook take the pull, so the only knot that matters is the one in the middle. Hair is slippery. If a hair slides off the pencil or the hook, that try doesn't count. Wind it again and try again.

flow.do: 1. Add coins gently, one at a time, counting out loud. 2. When the hair snaps, write the number. 3. Look closely, with the magnifier if you have one: where did it break? 4. Test all six hairs.
flow.say: Gently, one coin at a time. When it snaps, look closely. Where did it break?
flow.kid: Add coins one at a time. Count out loud. When it snaps, write the number. Look: where did it break?

chart.title: Made-up example results: six hairs from one person, 20 cm long
rows: at the knot, all three times

check.q: Where do knotted hairs usually break?
options: At the knot
At the top, under the book
Anywhere, by chance
check.why: At a knot, the hair is bent sharply round itself. The outside of each bend is stretched more than the rest of the hair. So the pull crowds there, like at the tip of a cut. The knot becomes the weakest spot. 'Anywhere, by chance' is what happens with plain hairs, which break at their own hidden weak spots.

flow.do: Talk together about knots in real ropes.
flow.say: The knot was made of the same hair. Nothing was taken away. So why do you think the knotted hair held fewer coins? Where would a climber check a rope most carefully?
flow.kid: Nothing was taken away from the knotted hair. So why was it weaker? Where should a climber check a rope?

ask.q: Where should a climber check a rope?
good: At the knots.
Where it bends sharply round something.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, you can add: a knot usually leaves a rope with only about half to three quarters of its strength, depending on the knot. Climbers and sailors choose knots carefully for this reason.
flow.think: A sharp bend weakened the hair. Where else might a sharp bend or corner be a weak spot? Think of a folded paper, or a bag's handle.

activities.title: Tap and Bend: testing without and with breaking

materials.item: a whole cup and a cracked cup, if you have one. No cracked cup? Use a steel tumbler and a piece of thread
a steel spoon for tapping
three paper clips of the same kind

activities.safety: A grown-up bends the paper clips. Broken ends are sharp, so wrap them in tape before throwing them away. Tap cups gently.

schedule.what: Tap pots and cups to hear hidden cracks. Count how many bends break a paper clip.

activities.record: Write how a whole cup and a cracked cup sounded. Write the number of bends for each paper clip, and the middle value.

flow.do: 1. Hang each cup from a finger by its handle. 2. Tap it gently with the spoon. 3. Listen to the ring. 4. No cracked cup? Hang a steel tumbler from a thread and tap it. Then hold it tightly in your hand and tap it again.
flow.say: Before you tap, guess. Which cup will ring clearly, and why? Now close your eyes and listen. Which one rings clearly? Which one sounds dull or buzzy?
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Tap each cup gently with a spoon. Which one rings? Which one buzzes?
flow.context: This is the first step of Tap and Bend. First you test cups and pots by tapping them, which does not harm them. Then you test paper clips by bending them until they break.
flow.parent: A whole cup rings clearly. A cracked cup sounds dull and buzzy. With the tumbler, the hand stops it vibrating freely, the way a crack does, so it sounds dull too. Tell your child that the tumbler shows the idea, but a real crack is what the tap test listens for.

flow.do: Talk about who uses the tap test.
flow.say: Potters tap new pots to find cracks. Long ago, railway workers called wheel tappers walked along trains at stations. They tapped each wheel with a hammer. A clear ring meant a sound wheel. A dull sound meant a crack.
flow.kid: Potters tap pots. Railway workers once tapped train wheels. A dull sound can mean a crack!

check.q: Why does a cracked cup sound dull when tapped?
options: The crack stops it ringing as one piece
Cracked cups are always lighter
The spoon is wrong
check.why: A whole cup vibrates all together and rings clearly. A crack breaks it into parts that vibrate separately, so the sound dies quickly and buzzes. Picking 'lighter' is a guess. A tiny crack hardly changes the weight at all.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up opens a paper clip into a straight piece. 2. Bend it at its middle, all the way one way and back again. That is one bend. 3. Count bends until it snaps. 4. Do the same with two more clips, bending the same way each time.
flow.say: One bend doesn't break it. Let's count how many it takes. Feel the bend after ten. Is it warm?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to bend the clip back and forth. Count each bend out loud. When does it snap?
flow.parent: Clips often snap after 10 to 30 bends. Each clip gives a different number, which is the point: tiny hidden flaws differ. This weakening is called fatigue. The bend gets warm because bending metal turns some of the movement into heat.

chart.title: Made-up example results: bends until a paper clip snapped

flow.do: Find the middle value of the three clips. Then talk about bridges and aeroplanes.
flow.say: Three clips, three different numbers. That's why engineers can't say exactly when a part will break. So they test many, and they check and replace parts long before.
flow.kid: Each clip broke at a different number. Find the middle one. Engineers check aeroplane parts long before they could break.
flow.think: Which is better for checking a bridge: a test that breaks it, or a test that doesn't? Why do engineers need both?

activities.context: This activity has two kinds of test. Tapping cups and pots checks for cracks without harming them. Bending paper clips until they snap shows how materials weaken after many bends.

setup.art: A railway wheel tapper of long ago tapping a train wheel with a long hammer, beside a potter tapping a clay pot.

activities.title: The Tiny Cut Test: what does one small cut do to a strip?

materials.item: one large paper napkin, separated into single layers (napkins have no perforations, which are weak lines)
a ruler, a pencil and scissors
sticky tape, a heavy book and a table
a small plastic bag with a paper clip opened into a hook
about 40 coins of one kind, all the same size and design, for example all one-rupee coins. Not enough coins? Use level spoonfuls of dry rice

activities.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors. Keep your feet away from under the bag. When the strip tears, the coins fall.

schedule.what: Cut six napkin strips and make a small cut in three of them. Test all six with coins, and see where each one tears.

activities.record: Make a table: strip (no cut or cut), coins held on each try, middle value, and where it tore. Then write what I think, what I saw, and why.
activities.context: This activity tests what one tiny cut does to a paper strip. You hang a bag from napkin strips, some with a small cut at one edge, and add coins until each one tears.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Tiny Cut Test. You guess, with a reason, what one small cut will do to a strip of paper.
flow.do: 1. Show your child two napkin strips, one plain and one with a small cut at one edge. 2. Ask the question below. 3. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: These strips are the same, except that one has a tiny cut at its edge. Will the cut strip hold more coins, the same, or fewer? Why do you think so? And where will it tear?
flow.kid: One strip has a tiny cut. One has none. Which will hold more coins? Why do you think so? Where will the cut strip tear?

good: Fewer, because there is less paper where the cut is.
Fewer, because it will start tearing at the cut.
The same, because the cut is so small.

flow.parent: Don't say what you expect. Any guess with a reason is a good start. The test will answer it.

flow.do: 1. On one layer of napkin, mark six strips, each 2 cm wide and 15 cm long, all in the same direction. 2. Cut them out slowly. 3. Throw away any strip with a nick. 4. On three strips, make one straight cut 5 millimetres long, in from one edge, halfway down.
flow.say: Same napkin, same size, same direction. The only thing we change is the tiny cut. Why does that make it a fair test?
flow.kid: Mark six strips, 2 cm wide and 15 cm long. Ask a grown-up to help cut. Make a tiny cut in three of them.
flow.parent: 5 millimetres is half a centimetre, a quarter of the strip's width. Measure it with the ruler, because a longer cut on one strip would be a change too.

flow.do: 1. Trap the top 3 cm of a strip under the heavy book, at the table's edge. 2. Fold the bottom 2 cm round the paper clip hook and tape it. 3. Hang the bag. 4. Add coins gently, one at a time, counting out loud. 5. When it tears, write the last number before it tore, and where it tore. 6. Test all six strips, a plain one and a cut one in turn.
flow.say: Gently, one coin at a time. Watch the cut closely as the bag gets heavier. What do you see?
flow.kid: Hang a strip. Add coins one at a time. Count out loud. Watch the cut. When it tears, write the number. Test all six.

ask.q: Where did the cut strips tear?
good: Right at the cut.
It started at the tip of the cut and ran across the strip.

flow.parent: The cut usually opens into a small V before the strip tears, and the tear runs across from its tip. A cut strip usually holds clearly fewer coins. Plain strips tear in different places, each at its own thin spot.

chart.title: Made-up example results: six strips from one napkin, 2 cm wide
rows: at the cut, all three times

flow.do: 1. Find the middle value for the plain strips and for the cut strips. 2. Ask your child to say three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Which strips held more? Where did the cut strips tear? Now tell me what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Find the two middle values. Which held more? Say what you think, what you saw, and why.

check.q: Napkin strips with a tiny cut held fewer coins, and they tore from the cut. Why?
options: The force of the pull crowded at the sharp tip of the cut, so the tear started there
The cut made the paper wet
The coins were heavier for the cut strips
check.why: When the bag pulls, the force crowds at the sharp tip of the cut. The paper there gives way first, and the tear runs across the strip. Picking 'heavier coins' is not possible, because every strip got the same coins.

flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: one tiny cut makes a strip much weaker. What I saw: the plain strips held about 21 coins, and the cut strips about 12. Every cut strip tore from its cut. Why: the force of the pull crowds at the tip of the cut, so the tear starts there and runs across. Keep this in mind for the Roots card.
flow.think: A milk packet has a small notch that says 'tear here'. Why does the notch help you open it?
