projects.title: Our Kitchen Towel Report

materials.item: kitchen towels of two or three different brands (call them Brand A, Brand B and Brand C), or kitchen towel, paper napkins and toilet paper
a measuring cup with millilitre marks
a bowl of water and a plate
a ruler, scissors, sticky tape, a paper clip hook, a small bag and one-rupee coins
the price and the number of sheets of each roll, from the packet

projects.safety: Wipe up spills so nobody slips. A grown-up helps with the scissors.

schedule.what: Test how much water one sheet of each towel soaks up. Test each three times.
Test how strong a wet strip of each towel is, with coins.
Work out the cost of one sheet. Write and share the report card.

projects.record: A report card with a table for each test, the cost per sheet, stars for each towel, and one sentence saying which towel you would buy and why.

flow.do: 1. Look at each packet together. 2. Write each brand's price and number of sheets. 3. Read any claims on the packet aloud, like 'super absorbent'.
flow.say: The packets make claims. Our job is to test them fairly, like a consumer scientist. That is a person who tests things that people buy.
flow.kid: Read the packets. What do they claim? You will test the claims, like a real consumer scientist.
flow.context: This is the first step of Our Kitchen Towel Report, a three-day project. You test real kitchen towels to find which soaks up most, which stays strongest when wet, and which is the best buy.

flow.do: 1. Pour 50 ml of water onto a plate. 2. Lay one whole sheet of Brand A on it for 10 seconds. 3. Lift it by one corner and let it drip back onto the plate for 5 seconds. 4. Pour what is left on the plate into the measuring cup. 5. 50 take away what is left is what the sheet soaked up. 6. Repeat three times for each brand.
flow.say: We pour the same 50 ml every time. Whatever is left behind tells us how much the sheet soaked up.
flow.kid: Pour 50 ml on a plate. Lay a sheet on it for 10 seconds. Lift it. Let it drip 5 seconds. Measure what is left. 50 take away that is what it soaked up.
flow.parent: If the sheets are different sizes, cut them all to the same size first, for example 20 cm by 20 cm. Otherwise the test is not fair.

chart.title: Made-up example: how much one sheet soaked up

flow.wait: Day 2: do this step the next day.
flow.do: 1. Cut a strip 2 cm by 15 cm from each brand. 2. Drip exactly 1 teaspoon of water along each strip. 3. Hang it from under a heavy book, like in the strip strength test. 4. Add coins gently until it tears. 5. Repeat three times for each brand.
flow.say: Kitchen towels get wet when we use them. So a fair test of strength should be done wet too.
flow.kid: Cut a strip of each towel. Drip one spoon of water on it. Hang a bag from it. Add coins until it tears. Do each brand three times.

check.q: Why test the kitchen towel strips wet, not dry?
options: Because kitchen towels are used wet, so the test should be like real use
Because wet paper is always stronger
To make the test faster
check.why: A good test is like the real job. Kitchen towels are used for wiping spills, so how strong they are when wet matters most. Picking 'wet paper is always stronger' is the opposite of what happens. Water loosens the grip between fibres, so most wet paper is weaker.

flow.wait: Day 3: do this step on the third day.
flow.do: 1. Work out the cost of one sheet: the price divided by the number of sheets. 2. Make a report card, with a table for each test and the cost per sheet. 3. Give each brand 1 to 3 stars for each test.
flow.say: The towel that soaks up most isn't always the best buy. What if it costs twice as much per sheet?
flow.kid: Work out the cost of one sheet. Price divided by number of sheets. Give each towel stars for each test.

chart.title: Made-up example report card

flow.do: Your child presents the report to the family, and says which towel they would buy and why.
flow.say: Which one would you buy? Is the winner the same if money is tight?
flow.kid: Show your report to your family. Which one would you buy? Why?
flow.think: Brand C was not the best at anything, but it was good at everything and cheap. Is that a kind of best?

challenges.title: Keep the Notebook Dry
challenges.problem: In the monsoon, school bags get soaked and notebooks get ruined. Design a cover for a notebook that keeps it dry when 50 ml of water is poured over it, and still works after it is opened 10 times.
constraints: You may use only one plastic bag, or none.
The cover must open and close, so the notebook can be used.
It must still keep the water out after being opened and closed 10 times.
Test it the fair way: the same 50 ml of water, poured from the same height, for every design.
materials: an old notebook, or a few sheets of paper folded and stapled as a test notebook
newspaper, cloth, wax crayons, a plastic bag, sticky tape, string and leaves
a measuring cup, a tray and a tissue to check for damp
general: Wrap the notebook in plastic, like a raincoat.
Use a zip bag or a plastic sleeve that closes.
Rub wax crayon thickly over paper to make waxed paper.
creative: Make it in layers, like Charles Macintosh's raincoat of 1823: something waterproof between two layers of cloth or paper.
Copy the lotus leaf: a waxy outer surface, so water rolls off.
Copy Kerala's old palm-leaf umbrellas and wrap it in big dried leaves, overlapping like roof tiles so water runs down and off.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own cover. Draw it, make it, open and close it 10 times, then pour the water. Put a dry tissue inside to check. Is it better than the others?

flow.do: 1. Pour 50 ml of water over an uncovered test notebook on a tray. 2. Look at how wet it gets.
flow.say: First, let's see the problem. This is what the monsoon does to a notebook with no cover.
flow.kid: Pour 50 ml of water over a notebook with no cover. How wet does it get?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Keep the Notebook Dry challenge. You design and test a monsoon cover for a notebook.

flow.do: Before making anything, draw two or three ideas and say which property each part needs.
flow.say: Engineers design before they build. Which parts must be waterproof? Which must bend?
flow.kid: Draw two or three ideas first. Which part keeps water out? Which part must bend to open?

flow.do: 1. Make your best design. 2. Open and close it 10 times. 3. Put a dry tissue inside. 4. Pour 50 ml of water over it from the same height. 5. Open it and check the tissue.
flow.say: Opening it ten times is part of the test. Real covers get used, not just looked at.
flow.kid: Make your cover. Open and close it 10 times. Put a tissue inside. Pour the water. Is the tissue dry?

check.q: Your cover kept the tissue dry when new, but after 10 openings the tissue got damp. What does that tell you?
options: The water was different
The folds or tape got weaker with use, so the test found a real problem
The test was unfair, so ignore it

challenges.title: The 100-Coin Strip
challenges.problem: A flat strip of toilet paper 2 cm wide holds only about 15 coins. Using just one sheet of toilet paper and a little tape, make something that holds 100 one-rupee coins.
constraints: You may use only one sheet of toilet paper, about 10 cm by 10 cm, and two small pieces of tape at the ends.
Hang it the same way as a normal strip: 3 cm trapped under the book and 2 cm folded round the hook.
Add coins the fair way: gently, one at a time.
materials: a heavy book, a paper clip hook and a small bag
about 100 coins of one kind, or as many as you have (count how many it held)
general: Fold the sheet into a thick, narrow strip, so there are many layers.
Roll it tightly into a thin tube.
Use the whole sheet, not just a 2 cm strip.
creative: Twist it into a rope. Rope-makers twist jute and coir fibres so they grip each other.
Cut it into three thin strips and plait them, like plaiting hair.
Twist two thin ropes, then twist them around each other the opposite way, as real ropes are made.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Make it, test it fairly, and write how many coins it held. Can you beat 100?

flow.do: Remind your child how many coins a flat 2 cm strip of toilet paper held. Or test one now.
flow.say: A flat strip held about 15 coins. Can the same sheet of paper hold 100, just by changing its shape?
flow.kid: A flat strip held about 15 coins. Can you make one sheet hold 100? Change its shape!
flow.context: This is the first step of the 100-Coin Strip challenge. You change the shape of one sheet of toilet paper to make it strong enough to hold 100 one-rupee coins.

flow.do: List three ideas together before trying any.
flow.say: Before you try, think like an engineer. Write three ideas.
flow.kid: Think first. Write or draw three ideas to make the paper stronger.

flow.do: 1. Make one idea. 2. Hang it 15 cm long. 3. Add coins gently, counting, until it breaks. 4. Try the next idea with a fresh sheet.
flow.say: Same paper, same length, same coins. Only the shape changes. That keeps it a fair test.
flow.kid: Make one idea. Hang it. Add coins until it breaks. Then try your next idea with a new sheet.

check.q: A twisted rope of toilet paper held 90 coins. A flat strip of the same sheet held 15. What made the difference?
options: The shape: twisting packs the fibres so they grip each other
The paper changed
The coins were lighter
check.why: It is the same paper and the same coins. Only the shape changed. Twisting squeezes the fibres together, so they grip each other and share the pull. Picking 'the paper changed' misses that we used the same kind of sheet. That is what made the test fair.

flow.parent: A twisted rope or a plait usually holds many times more than a flat strip. If 100 coins is too easy, try 200. If the tape at the ends tears first, that is the weakest part of the design, not the paper.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas together. Then talk about real ropes.
flow.say: People in India have twisted jute and coir into ropes for thousands of years. Each thin fibre is weak. Twisted together, they can tie up a boat.
flow.kid: Jute and coir ropes are made by twisting weak fibres together. Together, they can hold a boat!
flow.think: A flat strip tears at its one weakest spot. In a twisted rope, why might one weak fibre matter less?

challenges.title: Find the Crack Before It Grows
challenges.context: This is an engineering puzzle. A tiny crack can break a strong thing. How do engineers keep aeroplanes safe from cracks?
challenges.problem: An aeroplane is made of strong metal. But every flight bends its parts a little, and a tiny crack can start and slowly grow. Engineers must find cracks long before they are dangerous, even cracks too small to see. How would you do it?
constraints: You cannot break the part to look inside it.
The crack may be smaller than a hair.
Each check must be quick, because planes fly every day.
materials: an old cracked cup or plate and a whole one, if you have them
a little ink, and a damp cloth
a magnifying glass, if you have one
general: Look closely with eyes and a magnifying glass, on a fixed timetable.
Tap the part and listen. A cracked part sounds dull, like the cracked cup.
Paint on a coloured dye, wipe it off, and look. The dye stays in the crack and shows it as a dark line.
Send sound waves into the metal. A crack sends back an echo, like a doctor's scan of a baby.
Take an X-ray of the part, like an X-ray of a bone.
creative: Give windows and holes round corners, because cracks start at sharp corners. In 1954, two Comet airliners broke up in the air, and investigators traced the cause to cracks that grew from corners. Since then, plane windows have had round corners.
Add crack-stopper strips, so a crack that starts runs into a wall and stops.
Replace parts after a set number of flights, before cracks are likely.
Design every part so a crack grows slowly, and check often enough to catch it while it is still small.
challenges.your_turn: Invent your own way to find a hidden crack in something at home, like a cup, a bat or a chair. Draw it, try it, and explain how it works.

setup.caption: 1. Tap a whole cup and a cracked cup. Listen.

setup.caption: 2. Rub on ink, wipe it off, and look for a line.

flow.say: A plane bends a little on every flight. A tiny crack can start and slowly grow. How could engineers find it before it is dangerous? Guess first, and say why.
flow.kid: A plane can get tiny cracks. How would you find them? Guess, and say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Find the Crack Before It Grows puzzle.

flow.do: 1. Tap the whole cup with a spoon. 2. Tap the cracked cup the same way. 3. Ask which sounds different.
flow.say: Let's try one idea. Tap both cups the same way. What do you hear? Why might they sound different?
flow.kid: Tap both cups with a spoon. Which one sounds dull? Why?

check.q: The cracked cup sounds dull. Why?
options: The crack stops the cup ringing like one whole piece
The cracked cup is heavier
The spoon was different
check.why: A whole cup rings like one piece. A crack breaks the ring, so the sound dies quickly. Railway workers once tapped train wheels with hammers for this reason. Picking 'heavier' is a common guess, but a crack adds no weight.

flow.do: 1. Rub a little ink over the cracked plate or cup. 2. Wait one minute. 3. Wipe the surface clean with a damp cloth. 4. Look closely, with a magnifying glass if you have one.
flow.say: Now a second idea. The colour gets into the crack. When we wipe the top clean, the colour stays inside. What do you see?
flow.kid: Rub on the colour. Wait a minute. Wipe it off. Can you see a line?
flow.parent: The ink stays in the crack and shows it as a dark line. No cracked plate? Skip this step and read how engineers do it instead.

quiz.p: What makes a test fair?
opts: Changing only one thing and keeping everything else the same
Testing as many things as possible at once
Doing it as fast as you can
quiz.why: Only then do you know what caused the difference. Picking 'as many things as possible' usually means thinking more testing is always better. If many things change together, you can't tell which one mattered.

quiz.p: Before a test, Meena says: 'The wool will keep the rain out best.' What would make her guess more useful?
opts: Nothing, a guess is just a guess
Adding her reason, like 'because it is the thickest'
quiz.why: A guess with a reason can be checked. If thick cloth lets rain through, Meena learns that thickness was not the reason, and that is a real discovery. Picking 'look up the answer' skips the thinking that the test is for.

quiz.p: In the umbrella test, which of these must stay the same for every material?
opts: The amount of water poured on
quiz.why: The water poured on stays the same. The material is what we change. The water that comes through is what we measure. Picking 'the water that comes through' mixes up what we keep the same with what we measure.
quiz.context: This question is about the umbrella patch test. You stretch squares of old cloth over steel tumblers, let 20 ml of 'rain' drip onto each one, and after 4 minutes measure how much water came through.

quiz.p: Arjun pours 1 spoon of water on cotton and 3 spoons on plastic. What is wrong?
opts: Two things changed: the material and the amount of water
He should have used cold water
quiz.why: With two changes, we can't tell what caused the result. Picking 'nothing' usually means thinking any test that compares materials is fair.

quiz.p: Which tool would you use to measure how much water came through a cloth?
opts: A measuring cup with millilitre marks
quiz.why: Water is measured in millilitres with a measuring cup. A ruler measures length. A clock measures time, which we keep the same. Picking the clock mixes up what we time with what we measure.
quiz.context: This question is about the umbrella patch test. You stretch squares of old cloth over steel tumblers, let 20 ml of 'rain' drip onto each one, and after 4 minutes measure how much water came through.

quiz.p: A square of umbrella cloth let no rain through at all. Then a pin made one tiny hole in it, and it was tested again. Where did the rain come through?
opts: Nowhere, because the hole is so small
quiz.why: The rest of the cloth is still waterproof, but the hole is a gap. Drops form under the hole and fall. Picking 'nowhere' is a fair guess. A very tiny hole can hold water back for a while, but falling rain pushes water through it. Picking 'all over' forgets that the rest of the cloth has not changed.
quiz.context: This question is about the umbrella patch test. You stretch squares of old cloth over steel tumblers, let 20 ml of 'rain' drip onto each one, and after 4 minutes measure how much water came through.

quiz.p: Look at the chart. Which material soaked up water fastest?
quiz.why: Water climbed 9 cm up the kitchen towel, the highest. Picking printer paper often means the smallest number was read as the winner. Here, a taller bar means the water climbed higher.
quiz.context: This question is about the climbing water test. You hang strips of different materials with their ends in coloured water, and after 5 minutes measure how high the water climbed.

chart.title: Climbing water test: how high the water climbed in 5 minutes (made-up middle values)

quiz.p: Why should every column heading in a results table have a unit, like (cm)?
opts: So everyone knows what the numbers measure
Because units are always the same
quiz.why: A number like 12 could be 12 cm or 12 coins. The unit tells us. Picking 'to look neat' misses that a table is for others to understand.

quiz.p: Three tries gave 14, 15 and 3 coins. What is the middle value?
quiz.why: In order: 3, 14, 15. The middle is 14. Picking 3 usually means taking the last try. Picking 15 means taking the biggest.
quiz.context: This question is about the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a paper strip and add one-rupee coins, one at a time, until the strip tears.

quiz.p: In the tries 14, 15 and 3, the 3 is very different. What do scientists call it?
quiz.why: A result that does not fit with the others is an odd result, or anomaly. Scientists check what went wrong and test again. Picking 'prediction' mixes up what we guess before with what we get after.
quiz.context: This question is about the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a paper strip and add one-rupee coins, one at a time, until the strip tears.

quiz.p: A plastic bag let through no water, but it tears easily. What should you do before choosing it for an umbrella?
opts: Nothing, waterproof is all that matters
Test it for strength as well
quiz.why: One test checks one property. An umbrella must also be strong in the wind. Picking 'waterproof is all that matters' forgets that real jobs need several properties.

quiz.p: Look at the chart. Which paper would you choose for wiping up a big spill?
quiz.why: Kitchen towel held the most coins, so it is strongest, and it soaks up water fast. Picking toilet paper might come from it being softest. But it tore with the fewest coins.
quiz.context: This question is about the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a paper strip and add one-rupee coins, one at a time, until the strip tears.

chart.title: Strip strength test: coins held by strips 2 cm wide before tearing (made-up middle values)

quiz.p: Why does water roll off a lotus leaf?
opts: It is covered in tiny waxy bumps, and water clings to itself instead
The leaf has holes that drain the water
quiz.why: The drop rests on the tips of tiny waxy bumps, so it rolls away. Picking 'holes' is a natural guess. But if water went through holes, the leaf would get wet, and it stays dry.
quiz.context: Raindrops roll off lotus and arbi (colocasia) leaves in round, silver drops, and the leaves stay dry.

quiz.p: A napkin strip with a small cut held fewer coins than a strip with no cut. Why?
opts: The pull gathered at the sharp tip of the cut
The cut made the paper wet
The cut made the strip heavier
quiz.why: At a crack, the pull crowds into the sharp tip, so it tears from there. Picking 'heavier' is not possible, because cutting removes paper. It does not add any.
quiz.context: This question is about the Tiny Cut Test. You hang a bag from napkin strips, some with a small cut at one edge, and add coins until each one tears.

quiz.p: A plain hair held about 19 coins. A hair from the same person with a knot in it held about 13. Why did the knotted hair hold fewer?
opts: At the knot the hair is bent sharply, so the pull crowds there and it breaks
The knot made the hair shorter, so it was weaker
quiz.why: A sharp bend makes a weak spot, like the tip of a cut. The hair breaks there. Picking 'shorter' is a fair idea to check, but the strength of a hair doesn't depend on its length much. It breaks at its weakest spot. Picking 'older' misses that all the hairs came from the same person.
quiz.context: In the Knot Test, you hang a little cup of one-rupee coins from plain hairs and knotted hairs, and count the coins until each one snaps.

quiz.p: Engineers bent the wings of a new aeroplane until they snapped. Why break a perfectly good wing?
opts: To prove the wings are much stronger than they need to be, so planes are safe
quiz.why: Testing a few things until they break means the ones people fly in will not break. Picking 'faulty' gets it backwards. The test was to show the wings were good.

quiz.p: Can scientists predict exactly how many bends will snap a paper clip?
opts: No. Every clip has its own hidden flaws, so the number changes
quiz.why: Hidden flaws differ from clip to clip, so scientists can only say what usually happens. Picking 'always 10' means one try was taken as a rule. That is why we repeat tests.
quiz.context: In the tap and bend activity, a grown-up bends three paper clips back and forth and counts the bends until each one snaps.

quiz.p: In the muffle test, which cover usually makes the alarm quietest?
quiz.why: Soft, fluffy wool is full of fibres and air gaps, where the sound's vibration gets lost. Thin foil bounces much of the sound back instead. Picking foil is a common guess, because metal seems strong. But strong is not the same as good at absorbing sound.
quiz.context: In the muffle test, you cover a ringing phone alarm with different materials and measure how loud it still sounds.

quiz.p: A sponge springs back after squashing, but bread stays flat. What is springing back called?
quiz.why: A material that goes back to its old shape is elastic, like a rubber band or a sponge. Picking absorbent mixes up two sponge properties. A sponge is absorbent too, but that is about soaking up water, not springing back.
quiz.context: In the squash test, you press materials under the same three heavy books and measure whether they spring back.

quiz.p: Three strips cut from the same napkin, all 2 cm wide, held 18, 24 and 21 coins. Why were they different?
opts: Each strip had its own hidden weak spots, and tore at the weakest
The test was done wrong, so it should be thrown away
quiz.why: Paper has thin and thick patches. Each strip tears at its own weakest spot, so the numbers spread out. Picking 'the test was done wrong' throws away a real result. A spread like this is normal, and the middle value, 21, sums it up.
quiz.context: This question is about the width test. You cut strips from one paper napkin, some 2 cm wide and some 4 cm wide, hang a bag from each, and add one-rupee coins until it tears.

applications: Umbrellas, raincoats and school bag covers are made from materials that passed waterproof tests.
Helmets for scooters and motorbikes in India must pass tests and carry the ISI mark of the Bureau of Indian Standards.
Aeroplane wings, bridges and lifts are tested to much more than the biggest load they should ever carry.
Ropes for climbing, fishing and boats are tested until sample pieces break, so the rest can be trusted.
Kitchen towels, nappies and sanitary pads are tested for how much they soak up.
Cricket balls, bats and helmets are tested for hardness and strength.
Engineers test new bone screws and hip joints by loading them millions of times in machines.
Rail engineers check tracks and wheels for hidden cracks using ultrasound.
Potters tap pots, and builders tap tiles, to hear hidden cracks.
Consumer scientists test things people buy, like soaps and towels, to check the claims on the packets.
Packets have 'tear here' notches, which use a crack on purpose.
Self-cleaning paints and windows copy the waxy bumps of the lotus leaf.
Spider silk is tested in labs, so scientists can try to copy it for strong, light ropes and bandages.
New materials for spacecraft are tested outside the International Space Station, in the cold, heat and radiation of space.
Climbers and sailors check their ropes most carefully at the knots, because a knot is a weak spot.

open_questions.q: Can we ever predict exactly when a material will break?
open_questions.why_open: Every piece has its own hidden flaws, too small to see. Scientists can say what usually happens, but not exactly what one piece will do.

open_questions.q: Exactly how does the very first crack start inside a metal that is bent again and again?
open_questions.why_open: It starts with rows of atoms slipping, deep inside. Scientists study it with powerful microscopes and computers, and still argue about the details.

open_questions.q: How do spiders make silk so strong, from a liquid, at room temperature?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists understand parts of it. But nobody has yet made silk as good as a spider's, in large amounts.

open_questions.q: Is there a strongest possible material?
open_questions.why_open: New materials keep breaking records. Calculations suggest nuclear pasta in neutron stars may be strongest of all, but nobody can test it.

open_questions.q: How can we test materials that must last hundreds of years, like the walls of a nuclear waste store?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody can wait hundreds of years. Scientists speed up tests with heat and stress, and argue about whether fast tests really match slow time.

open_questions.q: How long does plastic really last in sun, soil and sea?
open_questions.why_open: Most plastics have only existed for about 70 years. The very long numbers you hear are estimates, still being tested.

open_questions.q: Why do some tests give different answers in different labs?
open_questions.why_open: Tiny differences in materials, tools and people's methods can change results. Scientists are still finding the best ways to make tests repeatable everywhere.

maths.problem: A toilet paper strip was tested three times. It held 14 coins, then 15 coins, then 3 coins. What is the middle value?
maths.explain: Put the three numbers in order, from smallest to biggest: 3, 14, 15. The one in the middle is 14. So the middle value is 14 coins. The 3 is an odd result, but it does not change the middle value much. If we added them all up and shared by 3, we would get only about 11, because the odd result pulls it down.
maths.context: This question is about the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a paper strip and add one-rupee coins, one at a time, until the strip tears.

answer_chart.title: Three tries with a toilet paper strip

maths.why_maths: Three tries give three numbers, but we need one number for each paper. Putting them in order and taking the middle one gives a fair single result that one fluke cannot spoil.

maths.problem: Here are some made-up results from the umbrella patch test. The middle values for rain that came through were: cotton hanky 12 ml, old jeans 3 ml, polyester dupatta 8 ml, woollen sweater 14 ml. Draw a bar chart. The sweater was the thickest cloth. Does the chart show that thick cloth keeps rain out best? What else could explain it?
maths.answer: No. The thickest cloth let the most rain through. Here is the bar chart. Something other than thickness must matter, such as the size of the gaps between the threads.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each cloth, as tall as its number. The tallest bar is the sweater, at 14 ml, and the shortest is the jeans, at 3 ml. If thick always meant waterproof, the sweater's bar would be the shortest. It is the tallest. So thickness is not the whole story. A knitted sweater has big holes between its loops. Jeans are woven tight.

maths.problem: Asha measured the rain that came through the cotton hanky with her small spoon: 4 spoons. Her father measured the same water with his big spoon: 2 spoons. Then they both used the medicine cup, and both got 12 ml. Why did the medicine cup agree, when the spoons did not?
maths.answer: Because a millilitre is the same size for everyone, but spoons are not.
maths.explain: Asha's spoon is smaller than her father's, so the same water fills more of her spoons. A millilitre is a standard unit. It is exactly the same amount on every medicine cup in the world. So both of them got 12 ml.
maths.context: This question is about the umbrella patch test. You stretch squares of old cloth over steel tumblers, let 20 ml of 'rain' drip onto each one, and after 4 minutes measure how much water came through.
maths.why_maths: Tests are only useful if other people can repeat them and compare. Standard units like the millilitre let everyone measure the same way.

maths.problem: Here are some made-up results from a width test. Strips 1 cm wide held about 9 coins. Strips 2 cm wide held about 20. If the pattern keeps going, how many will 4 cm strips hold? Then the 4 cm strips held 44. Was the pattern right? Why might the 1 cm strips have held a little less than half of 20?
maths.answer: The pattern predicts about 40 coins for 4 cm. The real middle value was 44, which is close. The 1 cm strips may have held less than half because their cut edges are a bigger part of them.
maths.explain: Doubling the width roughly doubles the coins: 20 + 20 = 40. The test gave 44, so the pattern was close but not exact. When you cut a strip, the fibres at both edges are cut and weakened. In a 1 cm strip, those damaged edges are a big part of the strip. In a 4 cm strip, they are a small part. So narrow strips hold a little less than the pattern says.
maths.context: This question is about the width test. You cut strips from one paper napkin, some 2 cm wide and some 4 cm wide, hang a bag from each, and add one-rupee coins until it tears.

answer_chart.title: Width test: predicted and measured (made-up results)

maths.why_maths: A pattern lets you predict before you test. When the test doesn't match exactly, the difference is a clue about what else is going on.

maths.problem: Brand A kitchen towel costs 120 rupees for 60 sheets. Brand C costs 60 rupees for 60 sheets. How much does one sheet of each cost? Which is the better buy, if both soak up about the same?
maths.answer: Brand A costs 2 rupees a sheet. Brand C costs 1 rupee a sheet. Brand C is the better buy.
maths.explain: To find the cost of one sheet, share the price by the number of sheets. 120 divided by 60 is 2, so Brand A is 2 rupees a sheet. 60 divided by 60 is 1, so Brand C is 1 rupee a sheet. If they soak up about the same, Brand C gives the same job for half the money.
maths.context: This is about Our Kitchen Towel Report project. You test kitchen towels fairly, then work out how much one sheet of each costs.
maths.why_maths: A test tells you which towel works best. Dividing the price by the number of sheets tells you which one gives the most for your money.

maths.problem: Look at the medicine cup in the picture. The big numbers are 0, 10 and 20 millilitres. Each small mark is 2 millilitres. How much rain came through the cotton hanky?
maths.explain: The water is past the 10 line. It reaches the first small mark above 10. Each small mark is 2 millilitres. So it is 10 + 2 = 12 millilitres.
maths.context: This question is about the umbrella patch test. You stretch squares of old cloth over steel tumblers, let 20 ml of 'rain' drip onto each one, and after 4 minutes measure how much water came through.

maths.why_maths: A measuring cup only helps if you can read it. Counting the small marks between the numbers turns the water level into an exact result for your table.

maths.problem: Five strips of the same kitchen towel held 52, 61, 58, 40 and 60 coins. A shop wants a towel strip that never tears below 45 coins. The middle value is 58. Is this towel safe to sell for that job? What would you tell the shop?
maths.answer: No. The middle value is well above 45, but one strip tore at 40. I would tell the shop that some strips are weaker than 45, so they need a stronger towel or more testing.
maths.explain: In order the results are 40, 52, 58, 60, 61, so the middle value is 58. But the shop's question is not about the middle. It is about the weakest strip. One strip in five held only 40, which is below 45. So about one strip in five might fail. A middle value hides the weakest result, and for safety the weakest result is the one that matters.
maths.context: This question is about the strip strength test. You hang a little bag from a paper strip and add one-rupee coins, one at a time, until the strip tears.
maths.why_maths: Ordering the results shows both the middle value and the weakest one. Which number matters depends on the question you are asking.

roots.context: We have tested cloths until rain came through, and paper strips until they tore. Now we ask what those tests tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A napkin strip with one small cut held fewer coins and tore at the cut. However strong a material is, a small crack can grow and break it. An object is only as strong as the crack it has. So engineers hunt for tiny cracks before they grow.
deep_truth.habit: We think strength belongs to the material: steel is strong and glass is weak. But a strong thing with a crack can break easily, and a thin glass thread with no cracks is very strong. So strength depends on the cracks as well as the material.
deep_truth.evidence: In the tiny cut test, napkin strips with one 5 mm cut tore at the cut and held fewer coins than strips with no cut. In 1920, Alan Arnold Griffith found that very thin glass threads were many times stronger for their size than thick rods, because they had fewer hidden cracks.

three.who_am_i: Running and jumping make tiny cracks in your bones every day. Your body finds those spots and rebuilds them.
three.what_is_life: A stone cannot mend its cracks. A living body keeps finding its weak spots and mending them, all its life.
three.what_is_this_world: In a cloth, a cup or a mountain, atoms hold their neighbours with the same electric force. A thing usually breaks where that hold is already broken: at a gap, a nick or a crack.

roots.thread: Every material we tested is held together by the same force: the electric force between atoms. It holds cotton, paper, steel and the hair on your head. Yet these materials behave very differently, because their atoms are different and are arranged differently. Our tests showed one more difference: where the hold is missing. The gaps between a sweater's loops, a pinhole and the tip of a cut were the places where rain got in or a tear began.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha told the people of Kesaputta, called the Kalamas, not to believe something only because it is old, or written down, or said by a respected teacher. When you know for yourselves, by looking carefully, that something is true, then accept it.
teachings.link: This is the spirit of a fair test. We did not believe the shopkeeper, or even our own first guess. We tested, and let the rain and the coins decide.

teachings.source: Thomas Reid, Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Man (1785)
teachings.teaching: The Scottish philosopher Thomas Reid wrote that a chain of reasoning can be no stronger than its weakest link, however strong the rest of it is.
teachings.link: Reid was writing about arguments, not materials. But our strips showed the same thing: each strip tore at its one weakest spot, however strong the rest of it was.

science.text: Real materials break at far smaller loads than the force between their atoms would allow, because breaking starts at tiny flaws. Griffith showed this with glass in 1920.
Nobody can predict exactly where and when one particular piece will break. Scientists can only say how often pieces of a kind break at each load.

other_view.who: Materials scientists who study tough materials
other_view.view: Not every material is ruled by its cracks in the same way. In glass, one tiny scratch can be enough to snap it. In rubber, cloth or soft metal, the material stretches at the tip of a crack and makes the tip blunt, so a small cut does much less harm. They would say that cracks matter in every material, but how much they matter depends on the material.

practice.title: Find the thin spots
practice.say: Take a paper napkin, or a sheet of paper, and hold it up to a window. Breathe in slowly, and out slowly. Look for the bright patches, where the fibres are thin, and the darker patches, where they are thick. Choose the spot where you think it would tear first. Now put the paper down. Rest one hand on your other arm, and feel the bone under the skin. Right now, your body is finding tiny cracks in that bone and mending them. Breathe in and out three times, and just notice your arm.
practice.kid: Hold a napkin up to the window. Breathe slowly. Find the thin, bright spots. Where would it tear first? Now hold your arm. Your body is mending tiny cracks in your bones right now. Breathe three times.
